cards.front: Name the seven SI base quantities and their units.
cards.back: • Length: metre (m), mass: kilogram (kg), time: second (s) • Current: ampere (A), temperature: kelvin (K) • Amount of substance: mole (mol), luminous intensity: candela (cd)
cards.hint: Mnemonic order: L-M-T-A-K-mol-cd.

cards.front: What is the difference between fundamental (base) and derived units?
cards.back: Base units are for the independent base quantities; derived units are combinations of base units (e.g. newton = $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$).

cards.front: Define the radian and the steradian.
cards.back: • Radian: $d\theta = \dfrac{ds}{r}$ (plane angle) • Steradian: $d\Omega = \dfrac{dA}{r^2}$ (solid angle) Both are dimensionless.
cards.hint: Full circle = $2\pi$ rad; full sphere = $4\pi$ sr.

cards.front: How is the SI second defined?
cards.back: Via the caesium-133 hyperfine transition frequency, fixed at 9 192 631 770 Hz (atomic clock).

cards.front: How is the SI metre defined?
cards.back: By fixing the speed of light in vacuum as 299 792 458 m/s; 1 m is the distance light travels in $1/299\,792\,458$ s.

cards.front: Which constant is fixed to define the kilogram in the revised SI?
cards.back: Planck's constant, $h = 6.626\,070\,15\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$.

cards.front: Values of 1 light year, 1 AU and 1 parsec in metres?
cards.hint: Trap: light year is a unit of distance, not time.

cards.front: Values of 1 fermi, 1 angstrom and 1 micron?
Powers of ten for the prefixes pico, nano, micro, mega, giga, tera?
Least count of a vernier callipers?
cards.back: LC = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = $\dfrac{\text{value of 1 MSD}}{\text{no. of vernier divisions}}$ (when N VSD = N−1 MSD).

cards.front: Least count of a screw gauge?
cards.back: LC = $\dfrac{\text{pitch}}{\text{no. of circular scale divisions}}$; pitch = linear distance moved per full rotation.

cards.front: How is zero error corrected in a vernier or screw gauge reading?
cards.back: True reading = observed reading − zero error (zero error taken with its sign).
cards.hint: Positive zero error is subtracted; negative zero error is effectively added.

cards.front: Distinguish accuracy and precision.
cards.back: • Accuracy: closeness to the true value • Precision: resolution / closeness of repeated readings (limited by least count)
cards.hint: A precise reading can still be inaccurate (e.g. due to zero error).

cards.front: What are systematic errors? Name their sources.
cards.back: Errors that tend to be in one direction (+ or −). • Instrumental errors • Imperfect technique / procedure • Personal errors

cards.front: What are random errors and how can they be reduced?
cards.back: Errors that occur irregularly in sign and size; reduced by repeating the measurement many times and taking the mean.

cards.front: What is least-count error and how can it be reduced?
cards.back: Error tied to the resolution of the instrument; reduced by using an instrument of higher precision (smaller least count) and better technique.

cards.front: Define absolute error and mean absolute error.
cards.back:
• Absolute error: $\Delta a_i = a_i - a_{mean}$
• Mean absolute error: $\Delta a_{mean} = \dfrac{\sum |\Delta a_i|}{n}$ (moduli used)
cards.hint: Trap: take magnitudes before averaging, else the mean is near zero.

cards.front: How is the result of repeated measurements reported?
cards.back: $a = a_{mean} \pm \Delta a_{mean}$, i.e. the true value likely lies between $a_{mean} - \Delta a_{mean}$ and $a_{mean} + \Delta a_{mean}$.

cards.front: Define relative error and percentage error.
cards.back: • Relative error = $\dfrac{\Delta a_{mean}}{a_{mean}}$ • Percentage error = $\dfrac{\Delta a_{mean}}{a_{mean}}\times 100\%$

cards.front: Maximum error in $Z = A + B$ or $Z = A - B$?
cards.back: $\Delta Z = \Delta A + \Delta B$ in both cases (absolute errors add).
cards.hint: Trap: for a difference the errors still ADD, never subtract.

cards.front: Maximum relative error in $Z = AB$ or $Z = A/B$?
cards.back: $\dfrac{\Delta Z}{Z} = \dfrac{\Delta A}{A} + \dfrac{\Delta B}{B}$ (relative errors add).

cards.front: Relative error in $Z = A^n$?
cards.back: $\dfrac{\Delta Z}{Z} = n\dfrac{\Delta A}{A}$

cards.front: Relative error in $Z = \dfrac{A^p B^q}{C^r}$?
cards.back: $\dfrac{\Delta Z}{Z} = p\dfrac{\Delta A}{A} + q\dfrac{\Delta B}{B} + r\dfrac{\Delta C}{C}$
cards.hint: Powers in the denominator also ADD their errors.

cards.front: If radius has 2% error, what is the error in volume of a sphere?
cards.back: $V \propto r^3$, so error = $3 \times 2\% =$ 6%.

cards.front: Percentage error in $g$ from $g = 4\pi^2 L/T^2$?
cards.back: $\dfrac{\Delta g}{g}\times100 = \left(\dfrac{\Delta L}{L} + 2\dfrac{\Delta T}{T}\right)\times100$; $4\pi^2$ adds no error.
cards.hint: The quantity with the highest power contributes most to the error.

cards.front: Which quantity should be measured most precisely in a formula?
cards.back: The one raised to the highest power, since its relative error gets multiplied by that power.

cards.front: Are zeros between non-zero digits and leading zeros significant?
cards.back: • Zeros between non-zero digits: significant • Leading zeros (e.g. in 0.0042): not significant

cards.front: Are trailing zeros significant?
cards.back: • With a decimal point (4.700): significant • Without a decimal point (4700): not significant as per NCERT
cards.hint: Use scientific notation ($4.700\times10^3$) to remove ambiguity.

cards.front: Number of significant figures in 0.05060 and in $6.320\times10^{4}$?
cards.back: • 0.05060 → 4 • $6.320\times10^{4}$ → 4 (power of 10 is not counted)

cards.front: Does changing units change the number of significant figures?
cards.back: No. 2.308 cm = 23.08 mm = 0.02308 m: all have 4 significant figures.

cards.front: Significant-figure rule for multiplication and division?
cards.back: Result keeps as many significant figures as the operand with the fewest significant figures.

cards.front: Significant-figure rule for addition and subtraction?
cards.back: Result keeps as many decimal places as the operand with the fewest decimal places.
cards.hint: Trap: count decimal places here, not significant figures.

cards.front: Give 436.32 g + 227.2 g + 0.301 g to correct precision.
cards.back: Sum = 663.821 g → rounded to one decimal place: 663.8 g.

cards.front: Rounding rule when the dropped digit is exactly 5?
cards.back: Preceding digit even → unchanged; odd → increased by 1. E.g. 2.745 → 2.74, 2.735 → 2.74.

cards.front: How many significant figures do exact numbers like 2 in $2\pi r$ have?
cards.back: Infinite; exact counting numbers and defined constants do not limit precision.

cards.front: What are the dimensions of a physical quantity?
cards.back: The powers (exponents) to which the base quantities are raised to represent that quantity, e.g. force $[MLT^{-2}]$.

cards.front: Dimensional formula of force, work and power?
cards.back: • Force: $[MLT^{-2}]$ • Work/energy: $[ML^2T^{-2}]$ • Power: $[ML^2T^{-3}]$

cards.front: Dimensional formula of pressure, stress and Young's modulus?
cards.back: All are $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$ (force per area).

cards.front: Dimensional formula of momentum and impulse?
cards.back: Both $[MLT^{-1}]$; SI unit $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$ = N s.

cards.front: Dimensional formula of Planck's constant $h$?
cards.back: $[ML^2T^{-1}]$, same as angular momentum (from $E = h\nu$).

cards.front: Dimensional formula of gravitational constant $G$?
Dimensions of surface tension and coefficient of viscosity?
cards.back: • Surface tension (force/length): $[MT^{-2}]$ • Viscosity $\eta$: $[ML^{-1}T^{-1}]$

cards.front: Dimensions of gas constant $R$ and specific heat capacity?
Which pairs of quantities share the same dimensions?
cards.back: • Work and torque $[ML^2T^{-2}]$ • Impulse and momentum • Angular momentum and $h$; frequency and angular velocity

cards.front: Name some dimensionless quantities.
cards.back: Strain, angle, refractive index, relative density, coefficient of friction.
cards.hint: Dimensionless does not always mean unitless: angle has unit radian.

cards.front: What quantity does $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$ represent dimensionally?
cards.back: Speed $[LT^{-1}]$; it equals the speed of light $c$.

cards.front: Which combinations of $R$, $L$, $C$ have dimensions of time?
cards.back: $RC$, $L/R$ and $\sqrt{LC}$ all have dimension $[T]$.

cards.front: State the principle of homogeneity of dimensions.
cards.back: Every term on both sides of a physical equation must have the same dimensions.
cards.hint: Only like quantities can be added, subtracted or equated.

cards.front: Uses of dimensional analysis?
cards.back: • Check consistency of equations • Derive relations among quantities • Convert units between systems

cards.front: Limitations of dimensional analysis?
cards.back: • Cannot find dimensionless constants • Fails for trig, log, exponential relations • Cannot derive relations with sums of terms

cards.front: Is a dimensionally correct equation always physically correct?
cards.back: No. A dimensionally wrong equation is surely wrong, but a dimensionally correct one may still be wrong (e.g. wrong constant).

cards.front: In $y = A\sin(\omega t - kx)$, dimensions of $\omega$ and $k$?
cards.back: Argument of sine is dimensionless: $\omega = [T^{-1}]$, $k = [L^{-1}]$.
cards.hint: Arguments of sin, cos, exp and log must always be dimensionless.

cards.front: Formula for converting a value from one unit system to another?
cards.back: $n_2 = n_1\left[\dfrac{M_1}{M_2}\right]^a\left[\dfrac{L_1}{L_2}\right]^b\left[\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}\right]^c$ for a quantity $[M^aL^bT^c]$.
cards.hint: Numerical value × unit stays constant: bigger unit, smaller number.

cards.front: 1 joule = how many erg?
cards.hint: Also 1 N = $10^5$ dyne.

cards.front: Use dimensions to find the period of a simple pendulum.
cards.back: $T \propto l^a g^b m^c$ gives $a = \tfrac12,\ b = -\tfrac12,\ c = 0$: $T = k\sqrt{l/g}$ ($k = 2\pi$ from theory).
cards.hint: Dimensional method cannot give the 2π.

cards.front: What is a frame of reference?
cards.back: A reference point (origin) with a set of axes and a clock used to describe position and time of an object.

cards.front: When can an object be treated as a point object?
cards.back: When the distance it moves is much larger than its size over a reasonable time.

cards.front: Difference between path length and displacement?
cards.back: • Path length: total distance covered, scalar, never negative • Displacement: change in position $\Delta x = x_2 - x_1$, can be +, − or 0

cards.front: How do magnitude of displacement and path length compare?
cards.back: $|\text{displacement}| \le \text{path length}$; equal only for motion in one direction along a straight line.

cards.front: A body returns to its starting point. Displacement and path length?
cards.back: Displacement = 0; path length = total distance travelled (non-zero).

cards.front: Define average velocity.
cards.back: $\bar v = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{x_2 - x_1}{t_2 - t_1}$; a vector, sign gives direction.

cards.front: Define average speed.
cards.back: Average speed = $\dfrac{\text{total path length}}{\text{total time}}$; scalar, never negative.

cards.front: How does average speed compare with magnitude of average velocity?
cards.back: Average speed ≥ |average velocity|; equal only if motion is in one direction.
cards.hint: Round trip: average velocity 0, average speed not 0.

cards.front: Average speed if equal distances are covered at speeds $v_1$ and $v_2$?
cards.back: $v_{av} = \dfrac{2v_1v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$ (harmonic mean).
cards.hint: Trap: not (v1+v2)/2 unless equal TIMES are spent.

cards.front: Average speed if equal time intervals are spent at $v_1$ and $v_2$?
cards.back: $v_{av} = \dfrac{v_1 + v_2}{2}$ (arithmetic mean).

cards.front: On an x–t graph, what gives the average velocity between two instants?
cards.back: The slope of the chord joining the two points on the x–t curve.

cards.front: Define instantaneous velocity.
cards.back: $v = \lim_{\Delta t\to 0}\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$

cards.front: How is instantaneous velocity found from an x–t graph?
cards.back: It is the slope of the tangent to the x–t curve at that instant.

cards.front: Is instantaneous speed equal to the magnitude of instantaneous velocity?
cards.back: Yes, always. (This need not hold for average speed and average velocity.)

cards.front: Shape of the x–t graph for a body at rest and in uniform motion?
cards.back: • At rest: line parallel to time axis • Uniform motion: straight inclined line (constant slope)

cards.front: Why can an x–t graph never be a vertical line?
cards.back: A vertical line means infinite velocity (and several positions at one instant), which is impossible.

cards.front: If $x = \alpha t^3$, find $v$ and $a$.
cards.back: $v = 3\alpha t^2$, $a = 6\alpha t$.

cards.front: What do a speedometer and an odometer measure?
cards.back: • Speedometer: instantaneous speed • Odometer: path length (distance covered)

cards.front: Define instantaneous acceleration; SI unit and dimensions?
cards.back: $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}$; unit $\text{m s}^{-2}$, dimensions $[LT^{-2}]$.

cards.front: Acceleration in terms of $v$ and $x$?
cards.back: $a = v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$; useful when $v$ is given as a function of position.

cards.front: What do the slope and area of a v–t graph give?
cards.back: • Slope: acceleration • Area under curve: displacement (area above axis +, below −)

cards.front: What does the area under an a–t graph give?
cards.back: Change in velocity in that time interval.

cards.front: When is a body speeding up or slowing down in 1-D?
cards.back: • $v$ and $a$ same sign: speeding up • $v$ and $a$ opposite signs: slowing down
cards.hint: Trap: negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down.

cards.front: Can velocity be zero while acceleration is non-zero?
cards.back: Yes. At the highest point of a vertical throw, $v = 0$ but $a = g$ downward.

cards.front: Shape of x–t graph for uniformly accelerated motion with $a>0$?
cards.back: A parabola curving upward (slope increases with time).
cards.hint: $a<0$: parabola curving downward.

cards.front: v–t graph for uniform motion and for constant acceleration?
cards.back: • Uniform motion: line parallel to time axis • Constant $a$: straight inclined line of slope $a$

cards.front: Can a speed–time graph go below the time axis?
cards.back: No. Speed is never negative; only a velocity–time graph can go below the axis.

cards.front: Three equations of motion for constant acceleration?
Displacement in terms of $u$, $v$ and $t$ for constant acceleration?
cards.back: $x = \dfrac{(u + v)}{2}\,t$; average velocity = $\dfrac{u+v}{2}$.
cards.hint: Only valid for uniform acceleration.

cards.front: Condition for the kinematic equations to hold?
cards.back: Acceleration must be constant (uniform) in magnitude and direction.
cards.hint: For variable $a$, integrate: $v = u + \int a\,dt$.

cards.front: Distance covered in the $n^{th}$ second?
cards.hint: Dimensionally fine: the hidden factor is 1 s.

cards.front: Graph of $v$ versus $x$ for uniform acceleration from rest?
cards.back: $v^2 = 2ax$: a parabola (with axis along $x$).

cards.front: How does stopping distance depend on initial speed?
cards.back: $d_s = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2a} \propto v_0^2$; doubling speed makes stopping distance 4 times.

cards.front: What is reaction time?
cards.back: Time taken by a person to observe, think and act; during it the vehicle keeps moving at constant speed.

cards.front: A bullet loses half its speed after penetrating $d$. How much further does it go?
cards.back: Further distance = $d/3$ (assuming constant retardation).

cards.front: Acceleration in free fall (NCERT value)?
cards.back: $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, downward, same for all bodies (air resistance neglected).
cards.hint: With upward positive, a = −g.

cards.front: Time and final speed for a body dropped from height $h$?
cards.back: • $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$ • $v = \sqrt{2gh}$

cards.front: State Galileo's law of odd numbers.
cards.back: For a body falling from rest, distances in successive equal time intervals are in ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 …

cards.front: Distance fallen in the $n^{th}$ second from rest?
Ratio of times to fall through successive equal heights from rest?
cards.back: $1 : (\sqrt2 - 1) : (\sqrt3 - \sqrt2) : \dots$

cards.front: Ball thrown up with speed $u$: maximum height and time to reach it?
Total time of flight and return speed for a ball thrown up with $u$?
cards.back: $T = \dfrac{2u}{g}$; it returns with the same speed $u$ (no air resistance).
cards.hint: Time of ascent = time of descent.

cards.front: Describe the v–t graph of a ball thrown vertically up.
cards.back: A straight line of slope $-g$, crossing the time axis at the top point ($t = u/g$).

cards.front: A packet is released from a balloon rising at speed $u$. Its initial velocity?
cards.back: $u$ upward (same as the balloon); it first rises, then falls.
cards.hint: Trap: it is not dropped 'from rest'.

cards.front: Ball thrown up at speed $u$ from a tower of height $h$. Equation to find time to hit ground?
cards.back: Taking up as positive: $-h = ut - \tfrac12 gt^2$

cards.front: Relative velocity of A with respect to B in 1-D?
cards.back: $v_{AB} = v_A - v_B$; and $v_{BA} = -v_{AB}$.

cards.front: Relative speed of two bodies moving in same vs opposite directions?
cards.back: • Same direction: $|v_A - v_B|$ • Opposite directions: $v_A + v_B$

cards.front: What do two parallel straight x–t lines show?
cards.back: Equal velocities, so relative velocity = 0; their separation stays constant.

cards.front: Relative acceleration of two freely falling bodies?
cards.back: Zero (both have $g$), so their relative velocity stays constant.

cards.front: Distinguish scalars and vectors with examples.
cards.back: • Scalar: magnitude only (mass, time, speed, work) • Vector: magnitude and direction, obeys vector addition (displacement, velocity, force)

cards.front: Is electric current a vector?
cards.back: No. It has direction but does not obey the laws of vector addition, so it is a scalar.
cards.hint: A vector must obey triangle/parallelogram law.

cards.front: What are position and displacement vectors?
cards.back: • Position vector $\vec r$: from origin to the point • Displacement: $\Delta\vec r = \vec r_2 - \vec r_1$, depends only on initial and final points

cards.front: When are two vectors equal?
cards.back: When they have the same magnitude and same direction (their location does not matter).

cards.front: Effect of multiplying vector $\vec A$ by a real number $\lambda$?
cards.back: Magnitude becomes $|\lambda| A$; direction same if $\lambda>0$, reversed if $\lambda<0$. Units change if $\lambda$ has units.

cards.front: Properties of the null (zero) vector?
cards.back: • $\vec A + \vec 0 = \vec A$ • $\lambda\vec 0 = \vec 0$, $0\vec A = \vec 0$ • Zero magnitude, direction undefined
cards.hint: Example: displacement after a round trip.

cards.front: State the triangle and parallelogram laws of vector addition.
cards.back: • Triangle: place tail of $\vec B$ at head of $\vec A$; resultant joins tail of $\vec A$ to head of $\vec B$ • Parallelogram: resultant is the diagonal from the common tail

cards.front: Which laws does vector addition obey?
cards.back: Commutative $\vec A + \vec B = \vec B + \vec A$ and associative $(\vec A+\vec B)+\vec C = \vec A+(\vec B+\vec C)$.
cards.hint: Vector subtraction is not commutative.

cards.front: Magnitude of the resultant of $\vec A$ and $\vec B$ at angle $\theta$?
cards.back: $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}$

cards.front: Direction of the resultant of $\vec A$ and $\vec B$ at angle $\theta$?
cards.back: $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{B\sin\theta}{A + B\cos\theta}$, $\alpha$ measured from $\vec A$.

cards.front: Maximum and minimum resultant of two vectors $A$ and $B$?
cards.back: • Max $A + B$ at $\theta = 0^\circ$ • Min $|A - B|$ at $\theta = 180^\circ$
cards.hint: Range: $|A - B| \le R \le A + B$.

cards.front: Resultant of two equal vectors of magnitude $A$ at angle $\theta$?
cards.back: $R = 2A\cos(\theta/2)$; at $120^\circ$, $R = A$.

cards.front: Magnitude of $\vec A - \vec B$ at angle $\theta$?
cards.back: $|\vec A - \vec B| = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 - 2AB\cos\theta}$

cards.front: Can two vectors of unequal magnitude add to zero? Three vectors?
cards.back: • Two unequal: never • Three: yes, if they form a closed triangle (coplanar)

cards.front: Resultant of vectors forming a closed polygon taken in order?
cards.back: Zero (polygon law of vector addition).

cards.front: Define a unit vector.
cards.back: $\hat A = \dfrac{\vec A}{|\vec A|}$: magnitude 1, only gives direction, no units or dimensions.

cards.front: Rectangular components of $\vec A$ making angle $\theta$ with x-axis?
cards.back: $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$, so $\vec A = A_x\hat i + A_y\hat j$.

cards.front: Magnitude and direction of $\vec A$ from its components?
cards.back: $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{A_y}{A_x}$

cards.front: Magnitude and unit vector of $\vec A = 3\hat i + 4\hat j$?
How are vectors added analytically?
cards.back: Add like components: $R_x = A_x + B_x$, $R_y = A_y + B_y$, $R_z = A_z + B_z$.

cards.front: Scalar (dot) product of $\vec A$ and $\vec B$?
cards.back: $\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\theta = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$; result is a scalar.
cards.hint: $\hat i\cdot\hat i = 1$, $\hat i\cdot\hat j = 0$.

cards.front: Condition for $\vec A \perp \vec B$ and the angle between them in general?
cards.back: • Perpendicular: $\vec A\cdot\vec B = 0$ • $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec A\cdot\vec B}{AB}$

cards.front: Vector (cross) product of $\vec A$ and $\vec B$?
cards.back: $|\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\theta$, direction ⊥ to both by right-hand rule; $\vec A\times\vec B = -\vec B\times\vec A$.
cards.hint: $\hat i\times\hat j = \hat k$; parallel vectors give $\vec 0$.

cards.front: Define velocity in a plane in component form.
cards.back: $\vec v = \dfrac{d\vec r}{dt} = v_x\hat i + v_y\hat j$, with $v_x = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$, $v_y = \dfrac{dy}{dt}$.

cards.front: Direction of instantaneous velocity relative to the path?
cards.back: Along the tangent to the path, in the direction of motion.

cards.front: Equations for motion in a plane with constant acceleration?
cards.back: • $\vec v = \vec v_0 + \vec a t$ • $\vec r = \vec r_0 + \vec v_0 t + \tfrac12\vec a t^2$
cards.hint: Each holds separately for x and y components.

cards.front: Key idea behind treating 2-D motion as two 1-D motions?
cards.back: Motions along x and y are independent; each obeys 1-D kinematics with its own acceleration component.

cards.front: Relative velocity of A with respect to B in a plane?
cards.back: $\vec v_{AB} = \vec v_A - \vec v_B$, and $\vec v_{BA} = -\vec v_{AB}$.

cards.front: Assumptions in the projectile motion analysis?
cards.back: Air resistance neglected and $g$ constant (uniform, vertically downward).

cards.front: Position of a projectile launched with speed $u$ at angle $\theta$?
cards.back: • $x = (u\cos\theta)\,t$ • $y = (u\sin\theta)\,t - \tfrac12 gt^2$

cards.front: Equation of trajectory of a projectile?
cards.back: $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{g x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$: a parabola.

cards.front: Time of flight of a projectile (ground to ground)?
cards.back: $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$

cards.front: Maximum height of a projectile?
cards.back: $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$

cards.front: Horizontal range of a projectile and its maximum?
cards.back: $R = \dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}$; maximum $R_{max} = \dfrac{u^2}{g}$ at $\theta = 45^\circ$.

cards.front: Which launch angles give the same range?
cards.back: Complementary angles $\theta$ and $(90^\circ - \theta)$, e.g. $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$.

cards.front: For complementary angles, relation of the two heights to range?
Relation between range and max height for a projectile?
cards.back: $R = 4H\cot\theta$; at $45^\circ$, $R_{max} = 4H$.
cards.hint: Also $\tan\theta = 4H/R$.

cards.front: Velocity and acceleration at the highest point of a projectile?
cards.back: • Velocity: $u\cos\theta$, horizontal • Acceleration: $g$ downward (never zero)
cards.hint: Velocity ⊥ acceleration only at the top.

cards.front: Which quantities stay constant during projectile motion?
cards.back: Horizontal velocity $u\cos\theta$ and acceleration $g$; vertical velocity and speed change.

cards.front: Kinetic energy at the top if launch KE is $K$ at angle $\theta$?
cards.back: $K\cos^2\theta$; at $45^\circ$ it is $K/2$.

cards.front: Speed and direction of a projectile when it lands at launch level?
cards.back: Same speed $u$, at angle $\theta$ below the horizontal.

cards.front: Body thrown horizontally at $u$ from height $h$: time and range?
cards.back: • $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$ • $R = u\sqrt{2h/g}$
cards.hint: Time of fall does not depend on $u$.

cards.front: One ball dropped, another thrown horizontally from same height. Which lands first?
cards.back: Both together; vertical motion is identical ($u_y = 0$) in both.

cards.front: What is uniform circular motion?
cards.back: Motion on a circle at constant speed; velocity direction changes, so it is accelerated.

cards.front: Magnitude and direction of centripetal acceleration?
cards.back: $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{R} = \omega^2R$, directed towards the centre.

cards.front: Relations between $v$, $\omega$, $T$ and $\nu$ in circular motion?
cards.back: • $v = \omega R$ • $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi\nu$

cards.front: Centripetal acceleration in terms of frequency $\nu$?
Is centripetal acceleration in uniform circular motion a constant vector?
cards.back: No. Its magnitude is constant but its direction keeps changing (always to centre).

cards.front: SI unit of angular velocity and its dimension?
cards.back: $\text{rad s}^{-1}$; dimension $[T^{-1}]$.

cards.front: Displacement and distance for half a revolution of radius $R$?
cards.back: Displacement $2R$; distance $\pi R$.
cards.hint: Full revolution: displacement 0, average velocity 0.

cards.front: What was Aristotle's fallacy about motion?
cards.back: He held that an external force is needed to keep a body moving uniformly. Wrong: force is needed only to change motion.
cards.hint: Bodies stop due to friction, not 'lack of force'.

cards.front: What did Galileo conclude from his double inclined plane experiments?
cards.back: With no friction, a ball would keep moving forever with constant velocity on a horizontal plane: the law of inertia.

cards.front: Define inertia. What measures it?
cards.back: Resistance of a body to change in its state of rest or uniform motion; measured by its mass.

cards.front: State Newton's first law of motion.
cards.back: A body stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted on by a net external force.

cards.front: Why are passengers thrown backward when a bus starts suddenly?
cards.back: Feet move with the bus, but the upper body tends to stay at rest due to inertia of rest.
cards.hint: Sudden braking → thrown forward (inertia of motion).

cards.front: Net force on a body moving with constant velocity?
cards.back: Zero; constant velocity means zero acceleration.
cards.hint: Trap: a moving body need not have a net force on it.

cards.front: What are inertial frames of reference?
cards.back: Frames that are not accelerating; Newton's laws hold in them.

cards.front: Define linear momentum; SI unit and dimensions?
cards.back: $\vec p = m\vec v$; unit $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$, dimensions $[MLT^{-1}]$.

cards.front: State Newton's second law.
cards.back: Rate of change of momentum equals applied force, in its direction: $\vec F = \dfrac{d\vec p}{dt}$.

cards.front: Form of the second law for constant mass?
cards.back: $\vec F = m\vec a$

cards.front: Define 1 newton. Relation to dyne?
cards.back: Force giving 1 kg an acceleration of $1\ \text{m s}^{-2}$; $1\ \text{N} = 10^5\ \text{dyne}$.

cards.front: Key features of $\vec F = m\vec a$ as NCERT stresses?
cards.back: • Vector law: holds component-wise • Local: $\vec a$ at a point depends on $\vec F$ at that point at that instant • Consistent with first law ($F=0 \Rightarrow a=0$)

cards.front: Does acceleration at an instant depend on past forces?
cards.back: No. It depends only on the net force at that instant; a stone dropped from a moving train has only $g$ after release.
cards.hint: Trap: the train's motion gives it horizontal velocity, not horizontal force.

cards.front: What does the slope of a momentum–time graph give?
cards.back: The net force acting on the body.

cards.front: Define impulse; SI unit?
cards.back: Impulse = $F\Delta t = \Delta p$ (change in momentum); unit N s = $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$.

cards.front: What does the area under a force–time graph give?
cards.back: Impulse, i.e. change in momentum.

cards.front: Why does a cricketer move hands back while catching a ball?
cards.back: It increases time of contact, so for the same $\Delta p$ the force $F = \Delta p/\Delta t$ is smaller.
cards.hint: Same idea: shock absorbers, sand pits, packing material.

cards.front: Impulse when a ball of mass $m$ hits a wall at $v$ and rebounds with $v$?
cards.back: $2mv$ (momentum changes from $+mv$ to $-mv$).
cards.hint: Trap: answer is not zero; momentum is a vector.

cards.front: Force on a gun firing $n$ bullets per second, each of mass $m$, speed $v$?
cards.back: $F = nmv$ (rate of change of momentum).

cards.front: State Newton's third law.
cards.back: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction: $\vec F_{AB} = -\vec F_{BA}$.

cards.front: Why don't action and reaction cancel each other?
cards.back: They act on two different bodies; only forces on the same body can cancel.

cards.front: Is there a cause–effect or time gap between action and reaction?
cards.back: No. They act simultaneously; either can be called action.

cards.front: Is the normal force on a book on a table the reaction to its weight?
cards.back: No. Reaction to weight is the book's pull on the Earth; reaction to normal force is the book's push on the table.
cards.hint: Weight and normal force act on the same body, so they can't be a pair.

cards.front: State the law of conservation of linear momentum.
cards.back: Total momentum of an isolated system (no net external force) remains constant.
cards.hint: Follows from Newton's second and third laws.

cards.front: Recoil velocity of a gun of mass $M$ firing bullet $m$ at $v$?
cards.back: $V = -\dfrac{mv}{M}$; minus sign: opposite to the bullet.

cards.front: Gun and bullet: equal momenta, but which has more kinetic energy?
cards.back: The bullet: $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so for equal $p$ the lighter body has more KE.

cards.front: A shell at rest explodes. Total momentum of the fragments?
cards.back: Zero; internal forces cannot change total momentum.

cards.front: Condition for equilibrium of a particle?
cards.back: Net external force is zero: $\vec F_1 + \vec F_2 + \dots = 0$.

cards.front: Condition for three concurrent forces to be in equilibrium?
cards.back: They must be coplanar and, drawn head to tail, form a closed triangle.

cards.front: Classify contact and non-contact forces with examples.
cards.back: • Contact: normal reaction, friction, tension, fluid forces • Non-contact: gravitational, electric, magnetic

cards.front: What is a free-body diagram?
cards.back: Diagram of one body alone showing only the forces acting on it, not forces it exerts.

cards.front: Tension in a light (massless) string over a frictionless pulley?
cards.back: Same throughout the string.

cards.front: Apparent weight in a lift accelerating up / down at $a$?
cards.back: • Up: $N = m(g + a)$ • Down: $N = m(g - a)$ • Free fall ($a = g$): zero
cards.hint: Lift at constant velocity: $N = mg$.

cards.front: Tension in a rope pulling mass $m$ upward with acceleration $a$?
Acceleration and tension for masses $m_1>m_2$ over a light pulley?
Force $F$ pushes $m_1$ which pushes $m_2$ on smooth floor. Contact force?
cards.back: $N = \dfrac{m_2F}{m_1 + m_2}$; common acceleration $a = \dfrac{F}{m_1 + m_2}$.

cards.front: Nature of static friction?
cards.back: Self-adjusting: equals the applied force up to a maximum $f_s^{max} = \mu_s N$ (limiting friction).

cards.front: Law of kinetic friction?
cards.back: $f_k = \mu_k N$, nearly independent of speed and of area of contact.

cards.front: How do $\mu_s$ and $\mu_k$ compare?
cards.back: $\mu_k < \mu_s$: harder to start motion than to keep it going.

cards.front: Describe the graph of friction vs applied force on a block.
cards.back: Friction rises linearly (= applied force) up to $\mu_sN$, then drops to constant $\mu_kN$ once sliding starts.

cards.front: Does friction always oppose motion?
cards.back: No. It opposes relative motion between surfaces; it can cause motion (walking, car accelerating: friction is forward).

cards.front: Block at rest on an incline of angle $\theta$: friction on it?
cards.back: $f = mg\sin\theta$ up the incline, which may be less than $\mu_sN$.
cards.hint: Trap: don't write $\mu_s mg\cos\theta$ unless motion is impending.

cards.front: Angle at which a block just starts sliding down an incline?
cards.back: $\tan\theta = \mu_s$ (angle of repose).

cards.front: Acceleration of a block sliding down a rough incline?
cards.back: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$

cards.front: Why is pulling a roller at an angle easier than pushing it?
cards.back: Pulling: $N = mg - F\sin\theta$ (less friction). Pushing: $N = mg + F\sin\theta$ (more friction). Pulling needs less force.

cards.front: How does rolling friction compare with sliding friction? How is friction reduced?
cards.back: Rolling friction is much smaller. Reduced by ball bearings, lubricants, air cushions.

cards.front: Dimensions of coefficient of friction? Can it exceed 1?
cards.back: Dimensionless; it can be greater than 1 for some surfaces.

cards.front: Force needed for uniform circular motion?
cards.back: Centripetal force $F_c = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2 r$, towards the centre.
cards.hint: Trap: not a new kind of force; provided by tension, friction, gravity, etc.

cards.front: Maximum safe speed of a car on a level circular road?
cards.back: $v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g}$; static friction provides the centripetal force.
cards.hint: Independent of the car's mass.

cards.front: Optimum speed on a banked road (no friction needed)?
cards.back: $v_0 = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$; normal force alone supplies centripetal force.

cards.front: Maximum safe speed on a banked road with friction?
cards.back: $v_{max} = \sqrt{rg\,\dfrac{\mu_s + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu_s\tan\theta}}$
cards.hint: Put $\mu_s = 0$ to get the optimum speed.

cards.front: Why are roads banked on curves?
cards.back: So that a component of the normal force provides centripetal force, reducing reliance on friction and wear of tyres.

cards.front: Define the scalar (dot) product of $\vec A$ and $\vec B$.
cards.back: $\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\theta = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$ • Result is a scalar • Commutative: $\vec A\cdot\vec B = \vec B\cdot\vec A$

cards.front: Values of $\hat i\cdot\hat i$ and $\hat i\cdot\hat j$?
cards.back: $\hat i\cdot\hat i = \hat j\cdot\hat j = \hat k\cdot\hat k = 1$ $\hat i\cdot\hat j = \hat j\cdot\hat k = \hat k\cdot\hat i = 0$ (perpendicular)
cards.hint: Dot product of perpendicular vectors is always zero.

cards.front: How do you find the angle between two vectors using the dot product?
cards.back: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec A\cdot\vec B}{AB}$ If $\vec A\cdot\vec B = 0$ (both non-zero), the vectors are perpendicular.

cards.front: Formula for work done by a constant force?
cards.back: $W = \vec F\cdot\vec d = Fd\cos\theta$ θ = angle between force and displacement. Work is a scalar.

cards.front: SI unit and dimensions of work (and energy)?
cards.back: joule (J) = N m Dimensions: $[ML^2T^{-2}]$

cards.front: Name three cases where a force acts but does zero work.
cards.back: • Displacement is zero (pushing a rigid wall) • Force perpendicular to displacement (centripetal force in circular motion) • Gravity on a body moving horizontally
cards.hint: Trap: holding a heavy bag still tires you, but does zero mechanical work on it.

cards.front: Sign of work done by kinetic friction on a sliding block, and by gravity on a rising ball?
cards.back: Both negative: force opposite to displacement ($\theta = 180^\circ$, $\cos\theta = -1$).

cards.front: Convert to joules: 1 eV, 1 erg, 1 calorie.
Is the kilowatt-hour (kWh) a unit of power?
cards.back: No, it is a unit of energy. 1 kWh = $3.6\times10^{6}$ J
cards.hint: Trap: kW is power; kW × h is energy (electricity bill unit).

cards.front: State the work-energy theorem.
cards.back: Change in kinetic energy = work done by the net force: $K_f - K_i = W_{net}$
cards.hint: Holds for all forces together, conservative or not.

cards.front: Relation between kinetic energy and linear momentum?
cards.back: $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so $p = \sqrt{2mK}$

cards.front: If the momentum of a body doubles, what happens to its KE?
cards.back: KE becomes 4 times ($K \propto p^2$ for fixed mass). If KE doubles, p becomes $\sqrt2$ times.

cards.front: Two bodies have equal kinetic energy. Which has more momentum?
cards.back: The heavier body: $p = \sqrt{2mK} \propto \sqrt m$

cards.front: Two bodies have equal momentum. Which has more kinetic energy?
cards.back: The lighter body: $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m} \propto \dfrac{1}{m}$
cards.hint: Gun and bullet after firing: equal momentum, bullet has far more KE.

cards.front: Speed of a body increases by 10%. Percentage increase in its KE?
cards.hint: Trap: answer is not 20%; the 2×(%) rule is only for small changes.

cards.front: Can kinetic energy ever be negative?
cards.back: No. $K = \frac12 mv^2 \ge 0$ always. Its value does depend on the frame of reference.

cards.front: Work done by a variable force $F(x)$ from $x_i$ to $x_f$?
cards.back: $W = \displaystyle\int_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x)\,dx$ = area under the F–x graph (area below the x-axis counts negative)
cards.topic: Work done by a variable force

cards.front: What does the area under a force–displacement graph give?
cards.back: The work done by that force over that displacement.
cards.hint: Slope of a work–time graph gives power.
cards.topic: Work done by a variable force

cards.front: For which forces can potential energy be defined?
cards.back: Only for conservative forces (gravity, spring force, electrostatic force).

cards.front: Properties of a conservative force?
cards.back: • Work depends only on initial and final positions, not on path • Work over any closed path is zero • Can be written as $F = -dV/dx$

cards.front: Name two non-conservative forces.
cards.back: Friction and air resistance (viscous drag). Work done by them depends on path and converts mechanical energy into heat.

cards.front: Relation between a conservative force and its potential energy $V(x)$ in 1D?
cards.back: $F(x) = -\dfrac{dV}{dx}$ Force points towards decreasing potential energy.

cards.front: Gravitational PE of mass m at small height h above the ground?
cards.back: $V = mgh$ (valid for $h \ll R_E$, g constant) Only differences in PE are physically meaningful; zero level is arbitrary.

cards.front: State the principle of conservation of mechanical energy.
cards.back: If only conservative forces do work, total mechanical energy $K + V$ stays constant.

cards.front: Ball dropped from height H. Its KE at height h above ground?
cards.back: $K = mg(H - h)$ Speed on reaching the ground: $v = \sqrt{2gH}$

cards.front: Body dropped from height H. At what height are its KE and PE equal?
cards.back: At $h = H/2$ (PE measured from the ground)

cards.front: Block slides from height h down different smooth inclines. Does the final speed depend on the path?
cards.back: No. $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ for every frictionless path; also independent of mass.
cards.hint: Time taken differs with the incline; speed at the bottom does not.

cards.front: Minimum speed at the top of a vertical circle (stone on a string, radius R)?
cards.back: $v_{top} = \sqrt{gR}$ At this speed the tension at the top is zero; gravity alone gives the centripetal force.

cards.front: Minimum speed at the lowest point for a string-bob to complete a vertical circle?
cards.back: $v_{bottom} = \sqrt{5gR}$ (from energy conservation with $v_{top} = \sqrt{gR}$)
cards.hint: Remember 5 at bottom, 1 at top (in units of gR for v²).

cards.front: Bob on a string in a vertical circle: difference between tension at bottom and top?
cards.back: $T_{bottom} - T_{top} = 6mg$ (for any speed, as long as the string stays taut)

cards.front: At critical speed in a vertical circle, ratio of KE at the lowest to the highest point?
Mass on a light rigid rod (not a string) in a vertical circle: minimum speed at the bottom?
cards.back: $2\sqrt{gR}$ A rod can push, so speed at the top may be zero: $v^2 = 4gR$.
cards.hint: Trap: $\sqrt{5gR}$ applies to a string, not a rod.

cards.front: State Hooke's law for a spring.
cards.back: $F_s = -kx$ k = spring constant (unit $\text{N m}^{-1}$); minus sign: force opposes displacement.

cards.front: Potential energy stored in a spring stretched or compressed by x?
cards.back: $V = \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ Same for extension and compression.

cards.front: Work done by the spring force as extension changes from $x_i$ to $x_f$?
cards.back: $W_s = -\dfrac{1}{2}k\left(x_f^2 - x_i^2\right)$ Over a cycle returning to $x_i$, net work by spring is zero (conservative).

cards.front: Spring stretched from 0 to x, then from x to 2x. Ratio of work done in the two steps?
cards.back: 1 : 3 $\frac12kx^2$ vs $\frac12k(4x^2 - x^2) = \frac32kx^2$

cards.front: Block of mass m moving at v hits a spring (constant k) on a smooth floor. Maximum compression?
cards.back: $x_m = v\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$ (from $\frac12mv^2 = \frac12kx_m^2$)

cards.front: Graphs for an ideal spring: F vs x and V vs x?
cards.back: • F vs x: straight line through origin, slope $-k$ • V vs x: parabola with minimum (zero) at $x = 0$

cards.front: Formulas for average and instantaneous power?
cards.back: $P_{av} = \dfrac{W}{t}$ $P = \dfrac{dW}{dt} = \vec F\cdot\vec v$

cards.front: SI unit and dimensions of power; value of 1 horsepower?
cards.back: watt (W) = $\text{J s}^{-1}$; dimensions $[ML^2T^{-3}]$ 1 hp = 746 W

cards.front: Motor lifts a lift of total mass M at constant speed v against friction f. Power needed?
cards.back: $P = (Mg + f)\,v$ Constant speed means motor force balances weight plus friction.

cards.front: Which quantities are conserved in every collision of an isolated system?
cards.back: • Total linear momentum • Total energy KE is conserved only in an elastic collision.

cards.front: Elastic vs inelastic vs perfectly inelastic collision?
cards.back: • Elastic: total KE conserved • Inelastic: some KE lost (heat, sound, deformation) • Perfectly inelastic: bodies stick together; maximum KE loss

cards.front: Is kinetic energy conserved during the contact time of an elastic collision?
cards.back: No. During contact some KE becomes deformation (potential) energy; only final KE equals initial KE.
cards.hint: Elastic means KE same before and after, not at every instant.

cards.front: Perfectly inelastic 1D collision: $m_1$ at $u_1$ hits $m_2$ at rest. Common velocity?
cards.back: $v = \dfrac{m_1u_1}{m_1 + m_2}$ (momentum conservation)

cards.front: KE lost when $m_1$ (speed $u_1$) sticks to $m_2$ at rest?
cards.back: $\Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}u_1^2$

cards.front: Elastic head-on collision, $m_2$ at rest: final velocities?
Elastic head-on collision between equal masses, one at rest. Result?
cards.back: They exchange velocities: moving body stops, the other moves off with $u_1$.
cards.hint: Snooker/Newton's cradle.

cards.front: Very heavy body hits a very light body at rest (elastic, head-on). Outcome?
cards.back: Heavy body continues with almost $u_1$; light body moves at about $2u_1$.

cards.front: Very light body hits a very heavy body at rest (elastic, head-on). Outcome?
cards.back: Light body rebounds with $-u_1$; heavy body stays almost at rest.
cards.hint: Ball bouncing off a wall.

cards.front: Why are light nuclei (heavy water, graphite) used to slow neutrons in a reactor?
cards.back: Energy transfer in an elastic collision is maximum when masses are nearly equal: a neutron gives far more of its KE to a deuteron than to a carbon nucleus.

cards.front: Fraction of KE transferred to a target at rest in an elastic head-on collision?
Elastic 2D collision of equal masses, one at rest (glancing). Angle between final velocities?
cards.back: $90^\circ$ ($\theta_1 + \theta_2 = 90^\circ$)

cards.front: Why can't 2D collision outcomes be found from conservation laws alone?
cards.back: Momentum (x, y) + energy give 3 equations but there are 4 unknowns; one quantity (e.g. an angle) must be known.

decks.title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

cards.front: Centre of mass of two particles $m_1$, $m_2$ on the x-axis?
cards.back: $X = \dfrac{m_1x_1 + m_2x_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ For equal masses it is the midpoint.

cards.front: Position vector of the centre of mass of n particles?
cards.back: $\vec R = \dfrac{\sum m_i\vec r_i}{M}$, where $M = \sum m_i$

cards.front: How do distances of two particles from their CM compare?
cards.back: Inversely as masses: $m_1r_1 = m_2r_2$ CM lies closer to the heavier particle.

cards.front: Centre of mass of a continuous body?
cards.back: $\vec R = \dfrac{1}{M}\displaystyle\int \vec r\,dm$ For uniform symmetric bodies it lies at the geometric centre.

cards.front: Where is the CM of a uniform rod, ring, disc, sphere, cylinder?
cards.back: At the geometric centre: midpoint of rod; centre of ring, disc, sphere; midpoint of cylinder's axis.

cards.front: Can the centre of mass lie outside the material of a body?
cards.back: Yes. E.g. a ring or a hollow sphere: CM is at the centre where there is no mass.

cards.front: Centre of mass of a uniform triangular lamina?
cards.back: At the centroid, the point where the medians meet.

cards.front: Equation of motion of the centre of mass of a system?
cards.back: $M\vec A = \vec F_{ext}$ CM moves like a single particle of mass M acted on by the net external force; internal forces cancel.

cards.front: A shell moving on a parabolic path explodes in mid-air. Path of its centre of mass?
cards.back: The CM continues on the same parabola, since the explosion forces are internal.
cards.hint: Fragments scatter; the CM does not care.

cards.front: Total linear momentum of a system in terms of its CM?
cards.back: $\vec P = M\vec V$ and $\dfrac{d\vec P}{dt} = \vec F_{ext}$ If $\vec F_{ext} = 0$, $\vec P$ and $\vec V$ are constant.

cards.front: A nucleus at rest decays into two fragments. What happens to the CM?
cards.back: CM stays at rest; the fragments fly off in opposite directions with equal and opposite momenta.

cards.front: Magnitude and direction of $\vec a\times\vec b$?
cards.back: $|\vec a\times\vec b| = ab\sin\theta$ Direction: perpendicular to the plane of $\vec a$ and $\vec b$, by the right-hand rule.

cards.front: Key properties of the vector (cross) product?
cards.back: • Not commutative: $\vec a\times\vec b = -\vec b\times\vec a$ • $\vec a\times\vec a = \vec 0$ • Distributive over addition

cards.front: Values of $\hat i\times\hat j$, $\hat j\times\hat k$, $\hat k\times\hat i$, $\hat i\times\hat i$?
cards.back: $\hat i\times\hat j = \hat k$, $\hat j\times\hat k = \hat i$, $\hat k\times\hat i = \hat j$ $\hat i\times\hat i = \vec 0$
cards.hint: Cyclic order i → j → k gives +; reverse order gives −.

cards.front: Relation between linear and angular velocity of a particle of a rotating body?
cards.back: $\vec v = \vec\omega\times\vec r$ Magnitude $v = \omega r_\perp$, $r_\perp$ = perpendicular distance from the axis.

cards.front: In rotation about a fixed axis, which is the same for all particles: v or ω?
cards.back: ω (angular velocity) is the same; linear speed $v = \omega r_\perp$ grows with distance from the axis.
cards.hint: Particles on the axis have v = 0.

cards.front: Define angular acceleration. Its direction for rotation about a fixed axis?
cards.back: $\vec\alpha = \dfrac{d\vec\omega}{dt}$ For a fixed axis, $\vec\omega$ and $\vec\alpha$ both lie along the axis.

cards.front: Define torque. SI unit and dimensions?
cards.back: $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$, $\tau = rF\sin\theta = r_\perp F$ Unit N m; dimensions $[ML^2T^{-2}]$

cards.front: Torque and work have the same dimensions. Are they the same kind of quantity?
cards.back: No. Torque is a vector (unit N m, never written J); work is a scalar.
cards.hint: Trap: same dimensions does not mean same physical quantity.

cards.front: When is the torque of a force about a point zero?
cards.back: • $F = 0$, or • the line of action passes through the point ($r_\perp = 0$, θ = 0° or 180°)

cards.front: Angular momentum of a particle. SI unit and dimensions?
cards.back: $\vec l = \vec r\times\vec p$, $l = rp\sin\theta$ Unit $\text{kg m}^2\text{s}^{-1}$ (= J s); dimensions $[ML^2T^{-1}]$
cards.hint: Same dimensions as Planck's constant.

cards.front: Relation between torque and angular momentum of a system?
cards.back: $\dfrac{d\vec L}{dt} = \vec\tau_{ext}$ Internal torques cancel in pairs (central internal forces).

cards.front: State the law of conservation of angular momentum.
cards.back: If the net external torque is zero, total angular momentum $\vec L$ of the system stays constant.

cards.front: Particle moving in a straight line with constant velocity: its angular momentum about a point off the line?
cards.back: Constant, $l = mvd$, where d = perpendicular distance of the line from the point.
cards.hint: Non-zero angular momentum does not need circular motion.

cards.front: What is a couple? Its net force and torque?
cards.back: Two equal, opposite, non-collinear forces. Net force zero; torque non-zero and the same about every point. Produces pure rotation.

cards.front: Conditions for mechanical equilibrium of a rigid body?
cards.back: • Translational: $\sum\vec F = 0$ • Rotational: $\sum\vec\tau = 0$ (about any point)

cards.front: State the principle of moments for a lever.
cards.back: Load × load arm = effort × effort arm: $F_1d_1 = F_2d_2$ Mechanical advantage = $\dfrac{\text{load}}{\text{effort}} = \dfrac{d_2}{d_1}$ (effort arm / load arm)

cards.front: Define the centre of gravity. When does it coincide with the centre of mass?
cards.back: Point about which total gravitational torque is zero. Coincides with CM when g is uniform over the body.

cards.front: When does the centre of gravity differ from the centre of mass?
cards.back: When g varies appreciably over the body, i.e. for very large extended bodies (e.g. a tall mountain).

cards.front: Define moment of inertia. SI unit and dimensions?
cards.back: $I = \sum m_ir_i^2$, $r_i$ = perpendicular distance from the axis Unit $\text{kg m}^2$; dimensions $[ML^2]$

cards.front: On what does the moment of inertia of a body depend?
cards.back: • Mass • Distribution of mass about the axis • Position and orientation of the axis
cards.hint: Trap: unlike mass, MI is not a fixed property of a body.

cards.front: Kinetic energy of a body rotating about a fixed axis?
cards.back: $K = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$
cards.hint: Rotational analogue of $\frac12mv^2$ with m → I, v → ω.

cards.front: Define radius of gyration.
cards.back: Distance k from the axis where the whole mass, if concentrated, gives the same MI: $I = Mk^2$, $k = \sqrt{I/M}$

cards.front: MI of a thin ring (M, R) about its central axis perpendicular to its plane? About a diameter?
cards.back: • Perpendicular axis: $MR^2$ • Diameter: $\dfrac{MR^2}{2}$

cards.front: MI of a uniform disc (M, R) about its central perpendicular axis? About a diameter?
cards.back: • Perpendicular axis: $\dfrac{MR^2}{2}$ • Diameter: $\dfrac{MR^2}{4}$

cards.front: MI of a thin rod (M, L) about a perpendicular axis through its centre? Through one end?
cards.back: • Centre: $\dfrac{ML^2}{12}$ • End: $\dfrac{ML^2}{3}$

cards.front: MI of a solid sphere and of a thin spherical shell about a diameter?
cards.back: • Solid sphere: $\dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$ • Thin spherical shell: $\dfrac{2}{3}MR^2$

cards.front: MI of a solid cylinder and a thin hollow cylinder about their own axis?
cards.back: • Solid cylinder: $\dfrac{MR^2}{2}$ • Thin hollow cylinder: $MR^2$
cards.hint: Solid cylinder = stack of discs; hollow cylinder = stack of rings.

cards.front: Radius of gyration of a disc about its central axis, and of a solid sphere about a diameter?
cards.back: • Disc: $\dfrac{R}{\sqrt2}$ • Solid sphere: $\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}}\,R$

cards.front: Ring and disc of same mass and radius: which has greater MI about the central axis?
cards.back: The ring ($MR^2$ vs $MR^2/2$): all its mass is at the maximum distance R.
cards.hint: Flywheels have heavy rims for this reason.

cards.front: State the theorem of perpendicular axes.
cards.back: $I_z = I_x + I_y$ Only for a planar lamina: x, y in its plane, z perpendicular, all three through one point.
cards.hint: Trap: not valid for 3D bodies like a sphere or cylinder.

cards.front: State the theorem of parallel axes.
cards.back: $I = I_{cm} + Ma^2$ a = distance between the given axis and the parallel axis through the CM. Valid for any body.
cards.hint: Trap: one of the two axes must pass through the CM.

cards.front: Of all parallel axes, about which is the MI of a body least?
cards.back: About the axis through the centre of mass (since $Ma^2 \ge 0$).

cards.front: MI of a ring about a tangent in its plane? About a tangent perpendicular to its plane?
cards.back: • Tangent in plane: $\dfrac{3}{2}MR^2$ • Tangent perpendicular to plane: $2MR^2$

cards.front: MI of a disc about a tangent in its plane? About a tangent perpendicular to its plane?
cards.back: • Tangent in plane: $\dfrac{5}{4}MR^2$ • Tangent perpendicular to plane: $\dfrac{3}{2}MR^2$

cards.front: MI of a solid sphere about a tangent?
Equations of rotational motion with constant angular acceleration?
cards.back: • $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$ • $\theta = \omega_0t + \frac12\alpha t^2$ • $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$

cards.front: Rotational analogues of mass, force, linear momentum and $P = Fv$?
cards.back: • m → I; F → τ; p → L • $P = Fv$ → $P = \tau\omega$; $\frac12mv^2$ → $\frac12I\omega^2$

cards.front: Newton's second law for rotation about a fixed axis?
cards.back: $\tau = I\alpha$ Analogue of $F = ma$.

cards.front: Work done and power delivered by a torque?
cards.back: • $W = \displaystyle\int \tau\,d\theta$ (= $\tau\theta$ for constant τ) • $P = \tau\omega$

cards.front: Mass m hangs from a string wound on a pulley (MI I, radius R). Acceleration of m?
cards.back: $a = \dfrac{mg}{m + I/R^2}$ (from $mg - T = ma$ and $TR = I\dfrac{a}{R}$)

cards.front: Angular momentum of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis?
cards.back: $L = I\omega$ (component along the axis)
cards.topic: Angular momentum about a fixed axis

cards.front: Why does a skater or diver spin faster on pulling in the arms?
cards.back: No external torque, so $I\omega$ is constant; pulling arms in lowers I, so ω increases.
cards.topic: Angular momentum about a fixed axis

cards.front: Rotational KE in terms of L. What happens to it if I halves at constant L?
cards.back: $K = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}$; with L constant, halving I doubles K. Extra energy comes from the internal work done by the skater.
cards.hint: Trap: L is conserved, KE is not.
cards.topic: Angular momentum about a fixed axis

cards.front: If Earth shrank to half its radius (same mass, uniform), length of the day?
cards.back: 6 hours $I \propto R^2$ falls to 1/4, so ω becomes 4 times and T = 24/4 h.
cards.topic: Angular momentum about a fixed axis

cards.front: State Kepler's first law (law of orbits).
cards.back: Every planet moves in an elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus.

cards.front: State Kepler's second law (law of areas).
cards.back: The line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time.

cards.front: Kepler's law of areas is a consequence of which conservation law?
cards.back: Conservation of angular momentum: gravity is a central force, so its torque about the Sun is zero.

cards.front: Areal velocity of a planet in terms of its angular momentum L?
cards.back: $\dfrac{dA}{dt} = \dfrac{L}{2m}$ = constant

cards.front: Where is a planet fastest in its orbit? Relation between speeds at perihelion and aphelion?
cards.back: Fastest at perihelion (closest to Sun). $v_Pr_P = v_Ar_A$ (angular momentum conservation)

cards.front: State Kepler's third law (law of periods).
cards.back: $T^2 \propto a^3$ T = period, a = semi-major axis of the orbit.

cards.front: If a planet's orbital radius becomes 4 times, its period becomes?
State Newton's universal law of gravitation.
cards.back: $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$ Attractive, along the line joining the two point masses; equal and opposite on each.

cards.front: Distance between two masses is halved. Gravitational force becomes?
cards.back: 4 times ($F \propto 1/r^2$)

cards.front: Does the gravitational force between two masses depend on the medium between them?
cards.back: No. It is independent of the intervening medium and of other bodies nearby.
cards.hint: Unlike the electrostatic force, which depends on the medium.

cards.front: Shell theorem: force on a point mass outside and inside a uniform spherical shell?
cards.back: • Outside: as if the shell's whole mass were at its centre • Inside: zero net force

cards.front: Nature of the gravitational force among fundamental forces?
cards.back: Weakest fundamental force; always attractive, central and conservative.

cards.front: Value, SI unit and dimensions of G?
Who first measured G experimentally, and how?
cards.back: Henry Cavendish (1798), using a torsion balance with large and small lead spheres.

cards.front: Difference between G and g?
cards.back: G is a universal constant (same everywhere). g is acceleration due to gravity, which varies with place.
cards.hint: Trap: g changes on the Moon; G does not.

cards.front: Acceleration due to gravity at Earth's surface in terms of G, $M_E$, $R_E$?
cards.back: $g = \dfrac{GM_E}{R_E^2}$ ≈ 9.8 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ Independent of the mass of the falling body.

cards.front: How can Earth's mass be found from g?
cards.back: $M_E = \dfrac{gR_E^2}{G}$ ≈ $6\times10^{24}$ kg

cards.front: Express g in terms of Earth's mean density ρ.
cards.back: $g = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi G\rho R_E$

cards.front: g at height h above Earth's surface?
cards.back: $g(h) = \dfrac{g}{(1 + h/R_E)^2}$ For $h \ll R_E$: $g(h) \approx g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R_E}\right)$
cards.hint: Trap: the approximation fails when h is comparable to R.
cards.topic: Variation of g with altitude & depth

cards.front: g at depth d below Earth's surface?
cards.back: $g(d) = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R_E}\right)$ Only the inner sphere of radius $R_E - d$ attracts (shell theorem).
cards.topic: Variation of g with altitude & depth

cards.front: Weight of a body at the centre of the Earth?
cards.back: Zero, since g = 0 there. Its mass is unchanged.
cards.topic: Variation of g with altitude & depth

cards.front: For small h, same decrease in g at height h and depth d. Relation between d and h?
cards.topic: Variation of g with altitude & depth

cards.front: At what height above the surface does g become g/4?
cards.hint: Trap: do not use the $1 - 2h/R$ approximation here.
cards.topic: Variation of g with altitude & depth

cards.front: At what depth does g become g/2?
cards.topic: Variation of g with altitude & depth

cards.front: Describe the graph of g versus distance r from Earth's centre.
cards.back: • Inside: increases linearly ($g \propto r$) from 0 at centre • Maximum at the surface • Outside: falls as $1/r^2$
cards.topic: Variation of g with altitude & depth

cards.front: Going up or going down from the surface: where does g decrease faster (small distances)?
cards.back: Going up: decrease $\propto 2h/R_E$, twice the rate of going down ($d/R_E$).
cards.topic: Variation of g with altitude & depth

cards.front: Gravitational potential energy of masses M and m separated by r?
cards.back: $V = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, taking V = 0 at $r = \infty$

cards.front: Why is gravitational potential energy negative?
cards.back: Zero is chosen at infinity and gravity is attractive; work must be done on the system to separate the masses to infinity.

cards.front: Increase in PE when mass m is raised from Earth's surface to height h?
cards.back: $\Delta V = \dfrac{GM_Emh}{R_E(R_E + h)}$ = $\dfrac{mgh}{1 + h/R_E}$ Reduces to mgh only for $h \ll R_E$.

cards.front: Define gravitational potential. Formula for a point mass M; SI unit?
cards.back: PE per unit mass: $-\dfrac{GM}{r}$ Scalar; unit $\text{J kg}^{-1}$; dimensions $[L^2T^{-2}]$

cards.front: Gravitational PE of a system of several particles?
cards.back: Sum over every pair: $V = -\sum \dfrac{Gm_im_j}{r_{ij}}$ (each pair counted once).

cards.front: Total gravitational PE of three masses m at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side l?
cards.back: $V = -\dfrac{3Gm^2}{l}$ (three pairs)

cards.front: Gravitational potential inside a uniform thin spherical shell (M, R)?
cards.back: Constant, equal to its surface value $-\dfrac{GM}{R}$, because the field inside is zero.
cards.hint: Zero field does not mean zero potential.

cards.front: Escape speed from Earth's surface: formula and value?
cards.back: $v_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM_E}{R_E}} = \sqrt{2gR_E}$ ≈ 11.2 km/s

cards.front: Does escape speed depend on the mass of the body or the direction of projection?
cards.back: No to both (ignoring air resistance). It depends only on the planet's mass and radius (and launch point).

cards.front: Why does the Moon have no atmosphere?
cards.back: Its escape speed is small (about 2.3 km/s); gas molecules with thermal speeds above this escape.

cards.front: Relation between escape speed and orbital speed just above Earth's surface?
cards.back: $v_e = \sqrt2\,v_o$ 11.2 km/s vs about 7.9 km/s

cards.front: Escape speed in terms of planet density ρ?
cards.back: $v_e = R\sqrt{\dfrac{8\pi G\rho}{3}}$ For equal density, $v_e \propto R$.

cards.front: Planet's radius doubles with mass unchanged. New escape speed?
cards.back: $v_e/\sqrt2$ ($v_e \propto \sqrt{M/R}$)

cards.front: Orbital speed of a satellite at height h above Earth?
cards.back: $v_o = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM_E}{R_E + h}}$ Independent of the satellite's mass. From $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$.

cards.front: Time period of a satellite at height h?
cards.back: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(R_E + h)^3}{GM_E}}$
cards.hint: This is Kepler's third law: $T^2 \propto r^3$.

cards.front: Period and speed of a satellite orbiting just above Earth's surface?
cards.back: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{R_E/g}$ ≈ 85 min Speed $\sqrt{gR_E}$ ≈ 7.9 km/s

cards.front: If a satellite moves to a larger orbit, what happens to its speed and period?
cards.back: Speed decreases ($v \propto 1/\sqrt r$); period increases ($T \propto r^{3/2}$).

cards.front: KE, PE and total energy of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r?
cards.back: • $K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ • $V = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ • $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$

cards.front: Relations between total energy, KE and PE of an orbiting satellite?
What does a negative total energy of a satellite signify?
cards.back: The satellite is bound to Earth. With E ≥ 0 it would escape to infinity.

cards.front: Minimum energy needed to make a satellite in orbit of radius r escape?
cards.back: $\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ (its binding energy, which makes E = 0)

cards.front: Energy needed to put a satellite of mass m from Earth's surface (at rest) into an orbit of radius r?
cards.back: $GM_Em\left(\dfrac{1}{R_E} - \dfrac{1}{2r}\right)$ (neglecting Earth's rotation)

cards.front: Define elasticity.
cards.back: Property of a body to regain its original size and shape when the deforming force is removed.

cards.front: Define plasticity. Give an example.
cards.back: Property of a body to not regain its original shape after the deforming force is removed (permanent deformation). E.g. putty, mud.

cards.front: Which is more elastic, steel or rubber?
cards.back: Steel. It has a much larger elastic modulus: it develops far more restoring stress for the same strain.
cards.hint: Trap: stretching easily does not mean more elastic.

cards.front: Microscopic origin of elasticity in solids?
cards.back: Atoms are held by interatomic forces that act like springs; when displaced, these forces restore them to equilibrium.

cards.front: Define stress. SI unit and dimensions?
cards.back: Restoring force per unit area: $\sigma = F/A$ Unit $\text{N m}^{-2}$ = Pa; dimensions $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$

cards.front: Three types of stress?
cards.back: • Longitudinal (tensile/compressive): force normal to area • Shearing (tangential): force parallel to area • Hydraulic: uniform pressure from all sides

cards.front: Define strain. Unit and dimensions?
cards.back: Fractional change in dimension (change ÷ original). A ratio: no unit, dimensionless.

cards.front: Formulas for longitudinal, shearing and volume strain?
cards.back: • Longitudinal: $\Delta L/L$ • Shearing: $\Delta x/L = \tan\theta \approx \theta$ • Volume: $\Delta V/V$

cards.front: Which stress and strain arise when a solid is immersed in a fluid under pressure?
cards.back: Hydraulic stress (equal to the pressure in magnitude) producing volume strain; shape is unchanged.

cards.front: State Hooke's law for solids.
cards.back: For small deformations, stress is proportional to strain: stress = k × strain k = modulus of elasticity.

cards.front: SI unit and dimensions of a modulus of elasticity?
cards.back: Same as stress: Pa ($\text{N m}^{-2}$), $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$, since strain is dimensionless.

cards.front: Which elastic modulus applies: stretching a wire, twisting/shearing a block, compressing a ball uniformly?
cards.back: • Stretching: Young's modulus Y • Shearing: shear modulus G • Uniform compression: bulk modulus B

cards.front: Stress-strain curve: what is the proportional limit?
cards.back: End of the initial straight-line region; up to here Hooke's law is obeyed.

cards.front: Stress-strain curve: what is the yield point (elastic limit)?
cards.back: Point up to which the body regains its shape on unloading; stress there = yield strength $\sigma_y$.

cards.front: What is permanent set?
cards.back: Residual strain left when a body loaded beyond its elastic limit is unloaded.

cards.front: What is ultimate tensile strength?
cards.back: Maximum stress a material can withstand (peak of the curve). Beyond it, fracture follows even if the load is reduced.

cards.front: How does the stress-strain curve distinguish ductile and brittle materials?
cards.back: • Ultimate strength and fracture points far apart: ductile • Close together: brittle

cards.front: What are elastomers? Give examples.
cards.back: Substances that can be stretched to large strains and still recover, though stress is not proportional to strain. E.g. rubber, tissue of the aorta.
cards.hint: Large elastic region, but Hooke's law is not obeyed over most of it.

cards.front: What does the slope of the linear part of a stress-strain graph give?
cards.back: The modulus of elasticity (Young's modulus Y for longitudinal stress).

cards.front: Define Young's modulus.
cards.back: $Y = \dfrac{F/A}{\Delta L/L} = \dfrac{FL}{A\,\Delta L}$ Ratio of tensile (or compressive) stress to longitudinal strain.

cards.front: Extension of a wire of length L, radius r under load F?
cards.back: $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{\pi r^2Y}$

cards.front: Same material and load; length and radius both doubled. New extension?
cards.back: Halved: $\Delta L \propto \dfrac{L}{r^2} = \dfrac{2}{4}$

cards.front: Does Young's modulus of a wire change if its length or thickness changes?
cards.back: No. Y depends only on the material (and its condition), not on dimensions.
cards.hint: Trap: extension changes with L and A; Y does not.

cards.front: Approximate Young's modulus of steel? Why is steel used in heavy machines?
cards.back: About $2\times10^{11}$ Pa. Metals like steel have large Y: they need large stress for small strain.

cards.front: Physical meaning of Y in terms of stress?
cards.back: Y equals the stress that would double the length (strain = 1), if Hooke's law held that far.

cards.front: Two wires of the same material and length, radii in ratio 1 : 2, same load. Ratio of stresses and of strains?
cards.back: Stress ratio 4 : 1; strain ratio also 4 : 1 (strain = stress/Y).

cards.front: Slope of the load (F) vs extension (ΔL) graph for a wire?
cards.back: $\dfrac{YA}{L}$ (the wire's effective spring constant)

cards.front: Define shear modulus (modulus of rigidity).
cards.back: $G = \dfrac{F/A}{\Delta x/L} = \dfrac{F}{A\theta}$ Ratio of shearing stress to shearing strain.

cards.front: Typical size of shear modulus compared to Young's modulus?
cards.back: For most materials $G \approx Y/3$.

cards.front: Define bulk modulus.
cards.back: $B = -\dfrac{p}{\Delta V/V}$ Ratio of hydraulic stress to volume strain.

cards.front: Why is there a minus sign in the bulk modulus formula?
cards.back: An increase in pressure decreases volume ($\Delta V$ is negative); the minus sign makes B positive.

cards.front: Define compressibility. Its SI unit?
cards.back: Reciprocal of bulk modulus: $k = \dfrac{1}{B}$ Unit $\text{Pa}^{-1}$ ($\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^2$).

cards.front: Order of bulk modulus for solids, liquids and gases?
cards.back: Solids > liquids > gases Gases are the most compressible.

cards.front: Which elastic modulus do liquids and gases possess?
cards.back: Only the bulk modulus. They cannot sustain shearing or longitudinal stress, so Y and G are not defined.
cards.hint: Fluids flow under shear.

cards.front: Elastic moduli of a perfectly rigid body?
cards.back: Infinite: any stress produces zero strain.

cards.front: Define pressure. Give its SI unit and dimensions.
cards.back: Normal force per unit area: $P = \dfrac{F}{A}$ (a scalar). • SI unit: pascal, $1\ \text{Pa} = 1\ \text{N m}^{-2}$ • Dimensions: $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$
cards.hint: Pressure has the same dimensions as stress and energy density.

cards.front: What is the density of water at 4 °C, and what are the units of relative density?
cards.back: • Density of water at 4 °C: $1.0 \times 10^3\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ • Relative density = $\rho_{substance}/\rho_{water(4^\circ C)}$: dimensionless, no unit

cards.front: State Pascal's law.
cards.back: Pressure in a fluid at rest is the same at all points at the same height, and a change in pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every point of the fluid and the container walls.

cards.front: Pressure at depth h below the open surface of a liquid of density ρ?
cards.back: $P = P_a + \rho g h$ • $P_a$ = atmospheric pressure • Gauge pressure: $P - P_a = \rho g h$

cards.front: Three vessels of different shapes and base areas hold water to the same height. Compare the pressure at their bases.
cards.back: Equal. Pressure depends only on depth ($\rho g h$), not on the shape or base area of the vessel (hydrostatic paradox).
cards.hint: Trap: the force on the base ($PA$) differs if areas differ; the pressure does not.

cards.front: Value of 1 atm in pascal and in mm of Hg?
cards.back: $1\ \text{atm} = 1.013 \times 10^5\ \text{Pa}$ = 760 mm of Hg (76 cm Hg) at sea level.

cards.front: How tall would a water barometer column be at 1 atm?
cards.back: About 10.3 m, from $h = \dfrac{P_a}{\rho_w g}$. Mercury ($\rho \approx 13.6$ times water) needs only 0.76 m.
cards.hint: Barometer: $P_a = \rho g h$; denser liquid, shorter column.

cards.front: What does an open-tube manometer measure?
cards.back: Gauge pressure: $P - P_a = \rho g h$, where h is the difference in liquid levels in the two arms.

cards.front: Working principle and force relation of a hydraulic lift?
cards.back: Pascal's law: equal pressure on both pistons. $F_2 = F_1 \dfrac{A_2}{A_1}$; mechanical advantage = $A_2/A_1$.

cards.front: Trap: does a hydraulic lift multiply energy?
cards.back: No, it multiplies only force. Equal volumes are displaced, $A_1 d_1 = A_2 d_2$, so the small piston moves farther and work in = work out (ideal).

cards.front: Principle of hydraulic brakes in vehicles?
cards.back: Pascal's law: pressure applied on the pedal's master cylinder is transmitted equally through brake oil to all wheel cylinders, so all wheels are braked equally.

cards.front: What is streamline (steady) flow?
cards.back: Flow in which the velocity at each point stays constant in time. Streamlines show the path of fluid particles and never cross each other.
cards.hint: If two streamlines crossed, a particle would have two velocities at one point.

cards.front: Equation of continuity for an incompressible fluid?
cards.back: $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$ ($Av$ = constant). It expresses conservation of mass; volume flux is the same at every cross-section.

cards.front: In a pipe with steady flow, the radius halves at a constriction. What happens to the speed?
cards.back: Speed becomes 4 times, since $v \propto \dfrac{1}{A} \propto \dfrac{1}{r^2}$.

cards.front: What is turbulent flow and when does it set in?
cards.back: Irregular flow with eddies and rapidly changing velocity at a point. It sets in when flow speed exceeds the critical speed, which is lower for wider tubes and less viscous fluids.

cards.front: State Bernoulli's equation.
cards.back: Along a streamline: $P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}$ It follows from the work-energy theorem (energy conservation) applied to a flowing fluid.

cards.front: Conditions under which Bernoulli's equation holds?
cards.back: • Steady (streamline) flow • Incompressible fluid • Non-viscous fluid (no energy lost to friction)
cards.hint: Trap: with viscosity, mechanical energy is lost and Bernoulli's equation does not hold exactly.

cards.front: What do the three terms of Bernoulli's equation represent?
cards.back: Each is energy per unit volume (units of pressure): • $P$: pressure energy • $\tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2$: kinetic energy • $\rho g h$: potential energy

cards.front: Torricelli's law: speed of efflux from a small hole at depth h below the open surface?
cards.back: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$, the same as the speed of a body falling freely through h (tank open to the air, top area much larger than the hole).

cards.front: Speed of efflux from a closed tank whose top is at pressure P, hole at depth h, outside at P_a?
cards.back: $v = \sqrt{2gh + \dfrac{2(P - P_a)}{\rho}}$ If $P = P_a$ it reduces to $\sqrt{2gh}$.

cards.front: What does Bernoulli's equation reduce to for a fluid at rest?
cards.back: With $v = 0$: $P_1 - P_2 = \rho g (h_2 - h_1)$, the ordinary hydrostatic pressure-depth relation.

cards.front: In horizontal flow, how are speed and pressure related? Give an example.
cards.back: Higher speed means lower pressure ($P + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^2$ = const). E.g. roofs blown off in storms, and the dynamic lift on an aircraft wing (faster air above, lower pressure above).

cards.front: What is viscosity?
cards.back: Internal friction in a fluid: the property that opposes relative motion between adjacent layers.

cards.front: Define the coefficient of viscosity η.
cards.back: $\eta = \dfrac{F/A}{v/l}$ = shearing stress / strain rate. F/A: tangential force per area; v/l: velocity gradient between layers.

cards.front: SI unit and dimensions of coefficient of viscosity?
cards.back: • SI unit: $\text{Pa s}$ (poiseuille, $\text{N s m}^{-2}$) • Dimensions: $[ML^{-1}T^{-1}]$ • CGS unit poise: 1 poise = 0.1 Pa s

cards.front: How does viscosity change with temperature for liquids and for gases?
cards.back: • Liquids: decreases as temperature rises • Gases: increases as temperature rises
cards.hint: Hot honey or oil flows faster; gases behave the opposite way.

cards.front: Velocity of liquid layers in viscous flow through a tube?
cards.back: Zero at the walls (layer in contact with wall at rest), increasing to a maximum along the axis.

cards.front: State Stokes' law.
cards.back: Viscous drag on a small sphere of radius a moving with speed v through a fluid: $F = 6\pi \eta a v$
cards.hint: Drag is proportional to radius and speed (not to $a^2$).

cards.front: Terminal velocity of a sphere (radius a, density ρ) falling through a fluid (density σ, viscosity η)?
cards.back: $v_t = \dfrac{2a^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}$ Reached when weight = buoyancy + viscous drag; net force and acceleration then zero.

cards.front: If the radius of a falling raindrop doubles, what happens to its terminal velocity?
cards.back: Becomes 4 times, since $v_t \propto a^2$.

cards.front: Terminal velocity when the sphere's density is less than the fluid's (ρ < σ)?
cards.back: $v_t$ is negative: the body rises at terminal speed, e.g. an air bubble in water.

cards.front: Graph of velocity vs time for a sphere dropped from rest in a viscous liquid?
cards.back: Velocity rises quickly at first, then levels off asymptotically at $v_t$; acceleration (slope) falls steadily to zero.

cards.front: Define surface tension. Give its SI unit and dimensions.
cards.back: Force per unit length acting along the liquid surface, normal to a line drawn on it: $S = F/l$. • SI unit: $\text{N m}^{-1}$ (= $\text{J m}^{-2}$) • Dimensions: $[MT^{-2}]$

cards.front: What is surface energy and how is it related to surface tension?
cards.back: Extra energy of molecules at the surface (fewer neighbours) compared with those inside. Work to increase area by $\Delta A$: $W = S\,\Delta A$, so S = surface energy per unit area.

cards.front: A soap film is held on a wire frame with a sliding wire of length l. Force due to surface tension on the slider?
cards.back: $F = 2Sl$, because the film has two surfaces.
cards.hint: Trap: forgetting the factor 2 for films and bubbles.

cards.front: Work done in blowing a soap bubble of radius r (surface tension S)?
cards.back: $W = 8\pi r^2 S$: two surfaces, each of area $4\pi r^2$.

cards.front: How does surface tension vary with temperature?
cards.back: It decreases as temperature rises (becomes zero at the critical temperature).

cards.front: Why do small liquid drops take a spherical shape?
cards.back: Surface tension makes the surface minimise its area, and a sphere has the least surface area for a given volume.

cards.front: What is the angle of contact? Give typical values for water-glass and mercury-glass.
cards.back: Angle between the liquid surface and the solid surface inside the liquid at the contact point. • Water-glass: acute, liquid wets glass • Mercury-glass: obtuse (about 140°), does not wet

cards.front: Relation between angle of contact and the interfacial tensions $S_{la}$, $S_{sa}$, $S_{sl}$?
cards.back: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{S_{sa} - S_{sl}}{S_{la}}$ • $S_{sl} > S_{sa}$: θ obtuse (no wetting) • $S_{sl} < S_{sa}$: θ acute (wetting)

cards.front: How do detergents and waterproofing agents affect the angle of contact?
cards.back: • Detergents/soaps: decrease θ, so water wets and penetrates fabric • Waterproofing agents: increase θ (made obtuse)

cards.front: Excess pressure inside a liquid drop of radius r?
cards.back: $P_i - P_o = \dfrac{2S}{r}$ (one surface).
cards.hint: Smaller drop, larger excess pressure.

cards.front: Excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius r?
cards.back: $P_i - P_o = \dfrac{4S}{r}$, because a soap bubble has two surfaces.

cards.front: Excess pressure inside an air bubble of radius r within a liquid?
cards.back: $\dfrac{2S}{r}$: an air bubble inside a liquid has only one liquid-air surface.
cards.hint: Trap: 4S/r only for a soap bubble in air (two surfaces).

cards.front: Height of capillary rise in a tube of radius a?
cards.back: $h = \dfrac{2S\cos\theta}{\rho g a}$ S: surface tension, θ: contact angle, ρ: liquid density.

cards.front: Capillary rise: what if the tube radius is halved? What happens with mercury?
