cards.back: • $h \propto 1/a$: halving radius doubles h • Mercury: θ > 90°, cos θ < 0, so level is depressed (capillary fall)

cards.front: Trap: a capillary tube is shorter than the rise height h. Does water overflow from the top?
cards.back: No. Water rises to the top and the meniscus becomes flatter (larger radius of curvature) so that $hR$ stays constant; there is no fountain.

cards.front: Difference between temperature and heat?
cards.back: • Temperature: measure of hotness of a body; decides direction of heat flow • Heat: energy transferred between bodies because of a temperature difference

cards.front: Relation between Celsius and Fahrenheit scales?
cards.back: $\dfrac{t_F - 32}{180} = \dfrac{t_C}{100}$, i.e. $t_F = \tfrac{9}{5}t_C + 32$ Fixed points: ice 0 °C = 32 °F; steam 100 °C = 212 °F.

cards.front: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales read the same?
Relation between Kelvin and Celsius scales? Triple point of water in kelvin?
cards.back: • $T = t_C + 273.15$ • Triple point of water: 273.16 K (fixed point of the Kelvin scale) • Size of 1 K = size of 1 °C

cards.front: Ideal gas equation?
cards.back: $PV = \mu R T$ μ: number of moles, T in kelvin, $R = 8.31\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

cards.front: How is absolute zero found using a constant-volume gas thermometer?
cards.back: Pressure varies linearly with temperature; extrapolating the P vs t line to P = 0 gives −273.15 °C (absolute zero, 0 K) for all low-density gases.

cards.front: Coefficient of linear expansion: definition and unit?
cards.back: $\dfrac{\Delta l}{l} = \alpha_l \Delta T$ Fractional change in length per kelvin; unit $\text{K}^{-1}$.

cards.front: Relation between coefficients of linear, area and volume expansion for an isotropic solid?
cards.back: $\alpha_a = 2\alpha_l$ and $\alpha_v = 3\alpha_l$ So $\alpha_l : \alpha_a : \alpha_v = 1 : 2 : 3$.

cards.front: Coefficient of volume expansion of an ideal gas at constant pressure?
cards.back: $\alpha_v = \dfrac{1}{T}$ (from $PV = \mu RT$). It is not constant: it decreases as T rises.
cards.hint: At 0 °C: $1/273 \approx 3.7 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{K}^{-1}$, far larger than for solids.

cards.front: What is the anomalous expansion of water?
cards.back: Water contracts when heated from 0 °C to 4 °C, then expands above 4 °C. So water has its maximum density at 4 °C.

cards.front: Why do lakes freeze from the top, and how does aquatic life survive?
cards.back: As water cools below 4 °C it becomes lighter and stays on top, freezing first. Ice (a poor conductor) insulates water below, and the bottom stays near 4 °C.

cards.front: Thermal stress in a rod clamped rigidly at both ends when its temperature rises by ΔT?
cards.back: $\dfrac{F}{A} = Y \alpha_l \Delta T$ Independent of length. Y: Young's modulus, $\alpha_l$: linear expansivity.

cards.front: A metal plate with a hole is heated. Does the hole get bigger or smaller?
cards.back: Bigger. The hole expands as if it were filled with the same metal (every length scales by $1 + \alpha_l \Delta T$).
cards.hint: Trap: the hole does not shrink.

cards.front: A bimetallic strip is heated. Which way does it bend?
cards.back: It bends so that the metal with the larger α is on the convex (outer) side, because that metal expands more.

cards.front: Define heat capacity of a body.
cards.back: $S = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta T}$: heat needed to raise the body's temperature by 1 K. Unit: $\text{J K}^{-1}$; depends on mass and material.

cards.front: Specific heat capacity: formula, SI unit and dimensions?
cards.back: $s = \dfrac{1}{m}\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta T}$ • Unit: $\text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ • Dimensions: $[L^2T^{-2}K^{-1}]$

cards.front: Define molar specific heat capacity.
cards.back: Heat needed per mole per kelvin: $C = \dfrac{1}{\mu}\dfrac{\Delta Q}{\Delta T}$ Unit: $\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

cards.front: Specific heat of water and why it matters?
cards.back: $4186\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, very high compared with most substances. So water is a good coolant (car radiators) and moderates coastal climate.

cards.front: Why does a gas have two specific heats, and which is larger?
cards.back: Heat absorbed depends on conditions: constant pressure ($C_p$) or constant volume ($C_v$). $C_p > C_v$, since at constant P some heat does work in expansion.
cards.hint: For solids and liquids, $C_p$ and $C_v$ differ very little.

cards.front: Principle of calorimetry?
cards.back: In an isolated system, heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body (no heat escapes to surroundings).

cards.front: What happens to temperature while a substance changes state?
cards.back: It remains constant; heat supplied goes into changing the state (latent heat), not raising temperature.

cards.front: Latent heat: formula and SI unit?
cards.back: $Q = mL$: heat needed to change the state of mass m without temperature change. Unit: $\text{J kg}^{-1}$

cards.front: Latent heats of fusion and vaporisation of water?
cards.back: • Fusion (ice at 0 °C): $3.33 \times 10^5\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$ • Vaporisation (at 100 °C): $22.6 \times 10^5\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$

cards.front: Why does steam at 100 °C cause worse burns than water at 100 °C?
cards.back: Steam releases its latent heat of vaporisation ($22.6 \times 10^5\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$) on condensing, before cooling like water.

cards.front: Temperature vs heat supplied graph as ice is heated to steam: what do the parts show?
cards.back: • Flat parts: melting and boiling; length ∝ latent heat • Rising parts: slope = $\dfrac{1}{ms}$, so a smaller slope means larger specific heat
cards.hint: Boiling plateau is about 7 times longer than melting plateau (22.6 vs 3.33).

cards.front: Effect of pressure on the melting point of ice? Name the related phenomenon.
cards.back: Increasing pressure lowers the melting point of ice. Ice melts under pressure and refreezes when pressure is removed: regelation.
cards.hint: Skating works because ice under the blade melts.

cards.front: Effect of pressure on boiling point? Give an application.
cards.back: Boiling point rises with pressure. A pressure cooker cooks faster; at high altitude (low pressure) water boils below 100 °C.

cards.front: What is sublimation? Give examples.
cards.back: Direct change from solid to vapour without passing through the liquid state. e.g. dry ice (solid $\text{CO}_2$), iodine.

cards.front: Why does solid CO₂ sublime at 1 atm instead of melting?
cards.back: Its triple point is at 5.11 atm and −56.6 °C. Below 5.11 atm liquid $\text{CO}_2$ cannot exist, so at 1 atm it goes solid → vapour.
cards.hint: Triple point: all three phases coexist.

cards.front: Three modes of heat transfer? Which needs no medium?
cards.back: Conduction, convection, radiation. Radiation needs no medium (e.g. sunlight through vacuum).

cards.front: Rate of heat flow by conduction through a bar in steady state?
cards.back: $H = KA\dfrac{T_C - T_D}{L}$ K: thermal conductivity, A: cross-section, L: length, $T_C > T_D$.

cards.front: SI unit and dimensions of thermal conductivity K?
cards.back: • Unit: $\text{W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ • Dimensions: $[MLT^{-3}K^{-1}]$

cards.front: Two slabs of equal area in series (L₁, K₁ and L₂, K₂). Equivalent conductivity?
cards.back: Steady state: same H through both. $\dfrac{L_1 + L_2}{K_{eq}} = \dfrac{L_1}{K_1} + \dfrac{L_2}{K_2}$
cards.hint: Like resistors in series: thermal resistance $L/KA$ adds.

cards.front: Why are metals good conductors of heat, and gases poor?
cards.back: Metals have free electrons that carry energy quickly; gases have widely spaced molecules, so gases are poor conductors.
cards.hint: Copper-bottomed cooking pots; air trapped in wool insulates.

cards.front: What is convection, and in which media can it occur?
cards.back: Heat transfer by actual bulk motion of the material. Only in fluids (liquids and gases). • Natural: driven by gravity/buoyancy • Forced: by pump or fan

cards.front: Explain sea breeze and land breeze.
cards.back: • Day: land heats faster, warm air over land rises, cool air flows from sea to land (sea breeze) • Night: land cools faster, flow from land to sea (land breeze)

cards.front: What is thermal radiation, and how fast does it travel?
cards.back: Heat transfer by electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared), needing no medium; travels at the speed of light.

cards.front: What is a blackbody?
cards.back: A body that absorbs all radiation falling on it (absorptivity 1). A good absorber is also a good emitter, so a blackbody is also the best emitter.

cards.front: State the Stefan-Boltzmann law.
cards.back: Power radiated: $H = e\sigma A T^4$ (e = 1 for a blackbody, 0 < e < 1 otherwise) $\sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-4}$
cards.hint: T must be in kelvin.

cards.front: Net power radiated by a body at T in surroundings at T_s?
cards.back: $H = e\sigma A (T^4 - T_s^4)$

cards.front: If the absolute temperature of a body doubles, how does its radiated power change?
cards.back: Becomes 16 times, since $H \propto T^4$.
cards.hint: Trap: use kelvin; doubling 27 °C to 54 °C is not doubling T.

cards.front: State Wien's displacement law.
cards.back: $\lambda_m T = b$, where $\lambda_m$ = wavelength of maximum emission $b = 2.9 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m K}$

cards.front: As a blackbody gets hotter, how does the peak of its spectrum shift?
cards.back: $\lambda_m$ shifts to shorter wavelengths ($\lambda_m \propto 1/T$): a heated iron glows dull red, then orange-yellow, then white.

cards.front: Why are cooking utensils blackened at the bottom and kettles polished outside?
cards.back: Black surfaces are good absorbers (take in heat from flame); shiny surfaces are poor emitters (lose less heat by radiation).

cards.front: What is the greenhouse effect?
cards.back: Earth's surface re-emits absorbed sunlight as infrared; greenhouse gases ($\text{CO}_2$, $\text{CH}_4$, $\text{N}_2\text{O}$, water vapour) trap it, warming the atmosphere.

cards.front: When is a system in thermal (thermodynamic) equilibrium?
cards.back: When its macroscopic variables (pressure, volume, temperature, mass, composition) do not change with time.

cards.front: Distinguish an adiabatic wall from a diathermic wall.
cards.back: • Adiabatic wall: insulating; allows no heat flow • Diathermic wall: conducting; allows heat flow, so systems reach thermal equilibrium

cards.front: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics.
cards.back: If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. It leads to the concept of temperature.

cards.front: What makes up the internal energy of a gas?
cards.back: Sum of kinetic and potential energies of the molecules in the frame where the system's centre of mass is at rest. It excludes the KE of the system moving as a whole.
cards.hint: Trap: a moving container of gas does not have higher internal energy.

cards.front: Which of these is a state variable: internal energy, heat, work?
cards.back: Internal energy is a state variable (depends only on state). Heat and work are not; they are modes of energy transfer and depend on the path.

cards.front: Two ways of changing the internal energy of a gas in a cylinder?
cards.back: • Heat: put it in contact with a body at a different temperature • Work: move the piston (compress or let it expand)

cards.front: On what does the internal energy of an ideal gas depend?
cards.back: Only on temperature (no intermolecular forces, so no potential energy). So $\Delta U = 0$ in any process with no net change of T.

cards.front: State the first law of thermodynamics with NCERT sign convention.
cards.back: $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$ • ΔQ positive: heat supplied to the system • ΔW positive: work done by the system

cards.front: Work done by a gas in a volume change?
cards.back: $W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} P\,dV$ = area under the P-V curve. Positive for expansion, negative for compression.

cards.front: What principle does the first law express, and what can it not tell us?
cards.back: It is the law of conservation of energy. It does not give the direction of a process; that comes from the second law.

cards.front: Mayer's relation for an ideal gas?
cards.back: $C_p - C_v = R$ (molar specific heats)

cards.front: Ratio of specific heats γ?
cards.back: $\gamma = \dfrac{C_p}{C_v}$, always greater than 1 for a gas.

cards.front: Define 1 calorie. Value in joules?
cards.back: Heat needed to raise 1 g of water from 14.5 °C to 15.5 °C. 1 cal = 4.186 J (mechanical equivalent of heat).
cards.hint: A narrow range is specified because water's specific heat varies slightly with temperature.

cards.front: Trap: for an ideal gas, ΔU = μC_vΔT only in isochoric processes?
cards.back: False. U depends only on T, so $\Delta U = \mu C_v \Delta T$ holds for every process of an ideal gas.

cards.front: Distinguish extensive and intensive state variables, with examples.
cards.back: • Extensive (depend on size): internal energy U, volume V, mass M • Intensive (independent of size): pressure P, temperature T, density ρ
cards.hint: Split the system in two: extensive ones halve, intensive ones stay the same.

cards.front: What is an equation of state? Give an example.
cards.back: A relation connecting the state variables of a system, e.g. $PV = \mu RT$ for an ideal gas.

cards.front: What is a quasi-static process?
cards.back: An infinitely slow process in which the system passes through a succession of equilibrium states (P, T well defined at each step).

cards.front: Why can't a sudden (non-quasi-static) process be drawn as a curve on a P-V diagram?
cards.back: The intermediate states are not equilibrium states, so P and T are not well defined for the whole gas; only initial and final points can be marked.

cards.front: Shapes on a P-V diagram of isobaric, isochoric and isothermal processes?
cards.back: • Isobaric: horizontal line • Isochoric: vertical line • Isothermal (ideal gas): rectangular hyperbola ($PV$ = const)

cards.front: Isothermal process: what stays constant and what is ΔU?
cards.back: T constant, so $PV$ = constant (Boyle's law). For an ideal gas $\Delta U = 0$, so $\Delta Q = \Delta W$.

cards.front: Trap: in an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, is the heat absorbed zero since ΔT = 0?
cards.back: No. ΔU = 0, but heat absorbed equals the work done by the gas, $\Delta Q = W \neq 0$.

cards.front: Work done by an ideal gas in isothermal expansion from V₁ to V₂?
cards.back: $W = \mu R T \ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$ Positive for expansion ($V_2 > V_1$).

cards.front: Adiabatic process: define it and give the P-V relation.
cards.back: No heat exchange with surroundings ($\Delta Q = 0$), e.g. insulated walls or a very fast process. $PV^\gamma = \text{constant}$

cards.front: Adiabatic relation between T and V, and between P and T?
cards.back: • $TV^{\gamma - 1} = \text{constant}$ • $P^{1-\gamma}T^{\gamma} = \text{constant}$

cards.front: Work done by an ideal gas in adiabatic change from T₁ to T₂?
cards.back: $W = \dfrac{\mu R (T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}$ Equivalently $\dfrac{P_1V_1 - P_2V_2}{\gamma - 1}$.

cards.front: What happens to temperature in adiabatic expansion and compression? Why?
cards.back: With ΔQ = 0, $\Delta U = -W$: • Expansion (W > 0): gas cools • Compression (W < 0): gas heats up

cards.front: A monatomic ideal gas is compressed adiabatically to half its volume. Final temperature?
cards.back: $TV^{\gamma-1}$ = const with $\gamma = 5/3$: $T_2 = T_1 \cdot 2^{2/3} \approx 1.59\,T_1$

cards.front: Compare slopes of adiabatic and isothermal curves on a P-V diagram at the same point.
cards.back: Adiabatic is steeper by a factor γ: • Isothermal: $\dfrac{dP}{dV} = -\dfrac{P}{V}$ • Adiabatic: $\dfrac{dP}{dV} = -\gamma\dfrac{P}{V}$

cards.front: Which process is sudden expansion in an insulated container, and which is slow expansion in a conducting one?
cards.back: • Sudden or insulated: adiabatic (no time for heat flow) • Slow, with diathermic walls in contact with a reservoir: isothermal

cards.front: Isochoric process: work done and heat absorbed?
cards.back: V constant, so W = 0. All heat changes internal energy: $\Delta Q = \Delta U = \mu C_v \Delta T$
cards.hint: On a P-V diagram it is a vertical line: no area, no work.

cards.front: In an isochoric process, how does the pressure of an ideal gas vary with temperature?
cards.back: $P \propto T$ (T in kelvin); P-T graph is a straight line through the origin.

cards.front: Isobaric process: work done and heat absorbed?
cards.back: $W = P(V_2 - V_1) = \mu R (T_2 - T_1)$ $\Delta Q = \mu C_p \Delta T$

cards.front: In an isobaric process, what fraction of heat supplied goes into internal energy?
cards.back: $\dfrac{\Delta U}{\Delta Q} = \dfrac{C_v}{C_p} = \dfrac{1}{\gamma}$; the rest, $1 - \dfrac{1}{\gamma}$, goes into work.
cards.hint: Monatomic gas: 3/5 to U, 2/5 to work.

cards.front: Cyclic process: ΔU, and how is net work found?
cards.back: $\Delta U = 0$ (returns to initial state), so $\Delta Q = W$ = area enclosed by the P-V loop. Clockwise loop: net work done by gas is positive.

cards.front: Same expansion V₁ → V₂ from the same initial state: order of work done in isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic?
cards.back: $W_{isobaric} > W_{isothermal} > W_{adiabatic}$ Pressure stays highest in isobaric and falls fastest in adiabatic, so area under the curve follows this order.

cards.front: Compressing a gas from the same initial state to the same final volume: which needs more work, isothermal or adiabatic?
cards.back: Adiabatic. Its curve is steeper, so pressure rises more and the area under the curve is larger.

cards.front: Free expansion of an ideal gas into vacuum (insulated): find ΔQ, W, ΔU and the change in T.
cards.back: ΔQ = 0, W = 0, ΔU = 0, so T is unchanged. It is not quasi-static and is irreversible.
cards.hint: Trap: it is adiabatic, but $PV^\gamma$ = const does not apply.

cards.front: Molar heat capacity of a gas in isothermal and adiabatic processes?
cards.back: • Isothermal: infinite (heat flows with ΔT = 0) • Adiabatic: zero (ΔT with no heat)
cards.hint: $C = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{\mu\Delta T}$.

cards.front: State the Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law.
cards.back: No process is possible whose sole result is the absorption of heat from a reservoir and its complete conversion into work.

cards.front: State the Clausius statement of the second law.
cards.back: No process is possible whose sole result is the transfer of heat from a colder body to a hotter body.

cards.front: What is a reversible process, and when is it possible?
cards.back: A process that can be retraced so that both system and surroundings return to their original states. Needs it to be quasi-static with no dissipative effects (friction, viscosity).

cards.front: Give examples of irreversible processes.
cards.back: • Free expansion of a gas • Heat flow from hot to cold body • Work done against friction • Diffusion and mixing of gases
cards.hint: All natural (spontaneous) processes are irreversible.

cards.front: State Boyle's law and Charles' law.
cards.back: • Boyle: at constant T, $PV$ = constant • Charles: at constant P, $V \propto T$ (T in kelvin)

cards.front: Ideal gas equation in terms of number of molecules?
cards.back: $PV = Nk_BT$, or $P = nk_BT$ with n = N/V (number density) $k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1}$

cards.front: State Avogadro's hypothesis. Value of Avogadro's number?
cards.back: Equal volumes of all gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules. $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$; 1 mole occupies 22.4 L at STP.

cards.front: Dimensions of the gas constant R and Boltzmann constant k_B?
When does a real gas behave like an ideal gas?
cards.back: At low pressure and high temperature (low density), where molecules are far apart and intermolecular forces are negligible.

cards.front: Graph of PV/(μT) vs P for an ideal gas and a real gas?
cards.back: Ideal gas: horizontal straight line (= R). Real gases deviate, approaching ideal behaviour as P → 0.

cards.front: State Dalton's law of partial pressures.
cards.back: Total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting ideal gases = sum of their partial pressures: $P = P_1 + P_2 + \dots$

cards.front: P vs T graph for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume?
cards.back: Straight line which, extrapolated, meets P = 0 at 0 K (−273.15 °C).

cards.front: Number of molecules per m³ of an ideal gas at STP?
Key assumptions of the kinetic theory of an ideal gas?
cards.back: • Molecules are tiny; their size is negligible vs separations • Random motion; elastic collisions • No intermolecular forces except during collisions • Collision time negligible
cards.topic: Kinetic theory of an ideal gas

cards.front: Change in momentum when a molecule hits a wall elastically (velocity component v_x normal to wall)?
cards.back: $2mv_x$ (from $mv_x$ to $-mv_x$). This momentum transfer to the wall produces gas pressure.
cards.topic: Kinetic theory of an ideal gas

cards.front: Why is $\overline{v_x^2} = \tfrac{1}{3}\overline{v^2}$ in the kinetic theory of pressure?
cards.back: Molecular motion is random (isotropic), so $\overline{v_x^2} = \overline{v_y^2} = \overline{v_z^2}$ and they add to $\overline{v^2}$.
cards.topic: Kinetic theory of an ideal gas

cards.front: Kinetic theory expression for pressure of an ideal gas?
cards.back: $P = \tfrac{1}{3}nm\overline{v^2}$ n: number density, m: mass of molecule, $\overline{v^2}$: mean square speed.
cards.topic: Kinetic theory of an ideal gas

cards.front: Pressure of an ideal gas in terms of its density?
cards.back: $P = \tfrac{1}{3}\rho\overline{v^2}$ where ρ = nm.
cards.topic: Kinetic theory of an ideal gas

cards.front: Relation between PV and the total translational kinetic energy E of a gas?
cards.back: $PV = \tfrac{2}{3}E$ So pressure = $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of KE per unit volume.
cards.topic: Kinetic theory of an ideal gas

cards.front: Average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule?
cards.back: $\overline{KE} = \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$ Depends only on temperature: T measures the average KE of molecules.

cards.front: H₂ and O₂ are at the same temperature. Compare the average KE of their molecules.
cards.back: Equal. Average KE ($\tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$) depends only on T, not on mass. The lighter H₂ moves faster instead.

cards.front: Total translational KE of one mole of an ideal gas?
cards.back: $\tfrac{3}{2}RT$ (= $N_A \times \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT$).

cards.front: rms speed of gas molecules?
cards.back: $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3k_BT}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3P}{\rho}}$ m: molecular mass, M: molar mass (kg/mol).

cards.front: If absolute temperature becomes 4 times, what happens to v_rms?
cards.back: Doubles, since $v_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$.

cards.front: Trap: gas pressure is doubled at constant temperature. What happens to v_rms?
cards.back: No change. $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$ depends only on T; density doubles along with P, so $3P/\rho$ is unchanged.

cards.front: Ratio of v_rms of H₂ to O₂ at the same temperature?
cards.back: 4 : 1, since $v_{rms} \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{M}}$ and $\sqrt{32/2} = 4$.

cards.front: Why is the internal energy of an ideal gas purely kinetic?
cards.back: There are no intermolecular forces, so no intermolecular potential energy; U depends only on T.

cards.front: What is a degree of freedom of a molecule?
cards.back: An independent coordinate needed to describe its motion (translation, rotation, vibration). A free point particle has 3 translational degrees of freedom.

cards.front: State the law of equipartition of energy.
cards.back: In thermal equilibrium at T, energy is shared equally among all modes: each quadratic energy term (degree of freedom) has average energy $\tfrac{1}{2}k_BT$.

cards.front: Degrees of freedom of a rigid diatomic molecule?
cards.back: 5: 3 translational + 2 rotational.
cards.hint: Rotation about the molecular axis is ignored (negligible moment of inertia).

cards.front: Why does a diatomic molecule have only 2 rotational, not 3?
cards.back: Its moment of inertia about the line joining the atoms is negligible, so rotation about that axis contributes no energy.

cards.front: Average energy per molecule associated with one vibrational mode?
cards.back: $k_BT$: $\tfrac{1}{2}k_BT$ for kinetic + $\tfrac{1}{2}k_BT$ for potential energy (two quadratic terms).
cards.hint: Trap: a vibrational mode counts twice under equipartition.

cards.front: Monatomic ideal gas: U per mole, Cv, Cp and γ?
Rigid diatomic gas: Cv, Cp and γ?
Diatomic gas with vibration (non-rigid): Cv, Cp and γ?
cards.back: Vibration adds $k_BT$ per molecule: $C_v = \tfrac{7}{2}R$, $C_p = \tfrac{9}{2}R$, $\gamma = \tfrac{9}{7}$

cards.front: Polyatomic gas with f vibrational modes: Cv and Cp?
cards.back: 3 translational + 3 rotational + f vibrational modes: $C_v = (3 + f)R$, $C_p = (4 + f)R$

cards.front: Relation between γ and total degrees of freedom f (each worth ½k_BT)?
cards.back: $\gamma = 1 + \dfrac{2}{f}$ Monatomic f = 3 gives 5/3; rigid diatomic f = 5 gives 7/5.
cards.hint: More degrees of freedom, γ closer to 1.

cards.front: Molar specific heat of a solid by equipartition?
cards.back: $C = 3R$. Each atom oscillates in 3 dimensions with energy $3k_BT$, so $U = 3RT$ per mole (ΔV negligible, so $C_p \approx C_v$).
cards.hint: This is the Dulong-Petit value, about 25 J mol⁻¹K⁻¹.

cards.front: Molar specific heat of water by equipartition, treating it like a solid?
cards.back: Three atoms, each contributing 3R: $C \approx 9R \approx 75\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, close to the measured value.

cards.front: Why does the classical equipartition prediction of specific heat fail at low temperatures?
cards.back: Measured specific heats fall as T → 0 because some degrees of freedom get 'frozen'. Explaining this needs quantum theory.

cards.front: Mean free path of gas molecules?
cards.back: Average distance between successive collisions: $l = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,n\pi d^2}$ n: number density, d: molecular diameter.

cards.front: How does mean free path depend on pressure and temperature?
cards.back: Using $n = \dfrac{P}{k_BT}$: $l = \dfrac{k_BT}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^2 P}$, so $l \propto T/P$.

cards.front: If the molecular diameter doubles at the same number density, what happens to the mean free path?
cards.back: Becomes one-fourth, since $l \propto \dfrac{1}{d^2}$.

cards.front: Trap: a gas in a sealed rigid container is heated. Does the mean free path change?
cards.back: No. l depends on number density n, which is fixed in a sealed rigid container. (l ∝ T only when pressure is kept constant.)

cards.front: Periodic motion vs oscillatory motion?
cards.back: • Periodic: repeats itself after a fixed time interval • Oscillatory: periodic to-and-fro motion about a mean position Every oscillation is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory
cards.hint: Uniform circular motion is periodic but not oscillatory.

cards.front: Relation between frequency and time period? SI unit of frequency?
cards.back: $\nu = \dfrac{1}{T}$; SI unit hertz: $1\ \text{Hz} = 1\ \text{s}^{-1}$

cards.front: Is $\sin\omega t + \cos\omega t$ an SHM? Amplitude and period?
cards.back: Yes, SHM: $\sin\omega t+\cos\omega t=\sqrt{2}\sin(\omega t+\pi/4)$ Amplitude $\sqrt{2}$, period $2\pi/\omega$
cards.hint: $a\sin\omega t + b\cos\omega t$ is SHM with amplitude $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.

cards.front: Is $\sin^3\omega t$ periodic? Is it SHM?
cards.back: Periodic (period $2\pi/\omega$) but not SHM: it is a combination of $\sin\omega t$ and $\sin 3\omega t$
cards.hint: Sum of sinusoids of different frequencies: periodic, not SHM.

cards.front: Is $\cos\omega t+\cos 3\omega t+\cos 5\omega t$ an SHM?
cards.back: Periodic, not SHM; period $2\pi/\omega$ (period of the slowest term)

cards.front: Is $e^{-\omega^2t^2}$ or $1+\omega t+\omega^2t^2$ periodic?
cards.back: Neither is periodic: they never repeat their values at regular intervals

cards.front: Displacement equation of SHM (with symbol meanings)?
cards.back: $x(t)=A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ • $A$: amplitude • $\omega$: angular frequency • $\phi$: phase constant (initial phase)

cards.front: Phase vs phase constant in SHM?
cards.back: • Phase: $(\omega t+\phi)$, decides the state of motion at time $t$ • Phase constant: $\phi$, value of phase at $t=0$

cards.front: Relation of angular frequency with $T$ and $\nu$? Unit?
cards.back: $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi\nu$; SI unit $\text{rad s}^{-1}$

cards.front: Defining condition for SHM in terms of acceleration?
cards.back: $a=-\omega^2x$: acceleration proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position

cards.front: How is SHM related to uniform circular motion?
cards.back: Projection of a particle in uniform circular motion on any diameter executes SHM Radius = amplitude, angular speed of particle = $\omega$ of SHM
cards.hint: Reference circle method: the shadow of the particle does SHM.

cards.front: Is uniform circular motion itself an SHM?
cards.back: No. It is periodic, but it is not to-and-fro along a line; only its projection on a diameter is SHM

cards.front: Velocity in SHM as function of time and of displacement?
cards.back: • $v=-\omega A\sin(\omega t+\phi)$ • $v=\pm\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2}$

cards.front: Where is the speed maximum in SHM, and its value?
cards.back: $v_{max}=\omega A$ at the mean position ($x=0$); speed is zero at the extreme positions ($x=\pm A$)

cards.front: Acceleration in SHM and its maximum value?
cards.back: $a=-\omega^2A\cos(\omega t+\phi)=-\omega^2x$ $a_{max}=\omega^2A$ at the extremes; $a=0$ at mean position

cards.front: Phase relations between $x$, $v$ and $a$ in SHM?
cards.back: • $v$ leads $x$ by $\pi/2$ • $a$ leads $v$ by $\pi/2$ • $a$ and $x$ differ by $\pi$ (always opposite)

cards.front: Graph of velocity vs displacement in SHM?
cards.back: Ellipse: $\dfrac{x^2}{A^2}+\dfrac{v^2}{\omega^2A^2}=1$ (becomes a circle if $\omega=1$ in chosen units)

cards.front: Graph of acceleration vs displacement in SHM?
cards.back: Straight line through origin with slope $-\omega^2$
cards.hint: Negative slope because $a=-\omega^2x$.

cards.front: Time taken to go from mean position to $x=A/2$ in SHM?
cards.back: $T/12$; from $x=A/2$ to $x=A$ it takes $T/6$
cards.hint: $x=A\sin\omega t$: $A/2$ reached at $\omega t=\pi/6$.

cards.front: Distance and displacement covered in one full period of SHM?
cards.back: Distance $4A$; displacement zero

cards.front: Average speed over one full cycle of SHM?
cards.back: $\dfrac{4A}{T}=\dfrac{2A\omega}{\pi}$; average velocity over a full cycle is zero
cards.hint: Trap: average speed is not $v_{max}/2$.

cards.front: Force law for SHM and the relation between $k$, $m$ and $\omega$?
cards.back: $F=-kx$ with $k=m\omega^2$, so $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$

cards.front: Dimensions and SI unit of force (spring) constant $k$?
General formula for period of SHM from displacement and acceleration?
cards.back: $T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{|x|}{|a|}}$, equivalently $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$

cards.front: Does the time period of SHM depend on amplitude?
cards.back: No. $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ is independent of amplitude (SHM is isochronous)
cards.hint: Larger amplitude means larger speed, so the period stays the same.

cards.front: Kinetic energy of a particle in SHM at displacement $x$?
Potential energy of a particle in SHM at displacement $x$?
cards.back: $U=\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$ (taking $U=0$ at mean position)

cards.front: Total mechanical energy in SHM?
cards.back: $E=\tfrac{1}{2}kA^2=\tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2$, constant at every point

cards.front: At what displacement are KE and PE equal in SHM?
cards.back: $x=\pm\dfrac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$
cards.hint: Each is $E/2$ there: $\tfrac12kx^2=\tfrac14kA^2$.

cards.front: Fraction of energy that is kinetic at $x=A/2$?
With what frequency do KE and PE oscillate if SHM has frequency $\nu$?
cards.back: $2\nu$ (period $T/2$); total energy stays constant
cards.hint: Trap: KE goes max twice per cycle (both passes through mean position).

cards.front: If the amplitude of SHM is doubled, what happens to energy and period?
cards.back: Energy becomes 4 times ($E\propto A^2$); period unchanged

cards.front: Graphs of $U$, $K$ and $E$ vs displacement $x$ in SHM?
cards.back: • $U$: upward parabola, zero at $x=0$ • $K$: downward parabola, zero at $x=\pm A$ • $E$: horizontal straight line

cards.front: Time period of a mass $m$ on a spring of constant $k$?
cards.back: $T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$; independent of amplitude and of $g$

cards.front: If the mass on a spring is made 4 times, what happens to $T$?
cards.back: $T$ doubles, since $T\propto\sqrt{m}$

cards.front: Period of a vertical spring-mass system in terms of its static extension $l$?
cards.back: $kl=mg$, so $T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$; still same as $2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$
cards.hint: Gravity shifts the mean position only; it does not change the period.

cards.front: Effective spring constant of two springs in series?
cards.hint: Series springs combine like parallel resistors.

cards.front: Effective spring constant of two springs in parallel?
Mass $m$ between two springs $k_1$, $k_2$ fixed to walls on either side. Period?
cards.back: Both springs push/pull the same way: $k=k_1+k_2$ $T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k_1+k_2}}$
cards.hint: Trap: this is a parallel combination, not series.

cards.front: A spring of constant $k$ is cut into $n$ equal parts. Constant of each part?
cards.back: $nk$ (since $k\propto 1/\text{length}$); for halves, $2k$ and period becomes $T/\sqrt{2}$

cards.front: A spring-mass system and a pendulum are taken to the Moon. Effect on periods?
cards.back: Spring-mass: unchanged Pendulum: increases ($g_{moon}\approx g/6$, so $T$ about $\sqrt{6}$ times)

cards.front: Time period of a simple pendulum?
cards.back: $T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$, valid for small angular amplitude

cards.front: Restoring torque on a simple pendulum, and when is it SHM?
cards.back: $\tau=-mgL\sin\theta$; SHM only for small $\theta$ where $\sin\theta\approx\theta$ (in radians)

cards.front: On what does the period of a simple pendulum not depend?
cards.back: Mass of the bob and (for small oscillations) amplitude; depends only on $L$ and $g$

cards.front: What is a seconds pendulum? Its length?
cards.back: Pendulum with $T=2\ \text{s}$; length $L=gT^2/4\pi^2\approx$ 1 m (about 0.99 m for $g=9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$)

cards.front: Length of a pendulum is increased by 21%. Change in period?
cards.back: Increases by 10%: $T\propto\sqrt{L}$ and $\sqrt{1.21}=1.1$
cards.hint: For small changes: $\Delta T/T=\tfrac12\,\Delta L/L$.

cards.front: Graph of $T^2$ vs $L$ for a simple pendulum?
cards.back: Straight line through origin, slope $=\dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}$
cards.hint: Used to find $g$ in the lab.

cards.front: Length $L$ of a pendulum is measured from where to where?
cards.back: From the point of suspension to the centre of the bob (effective length)

cards.front: Period of a pendulum in a lift accelerating up / down with $a$, and in free fall?
cards.back: • Up: $T=2\pi\sqrt{L/(g+a)}$ • Down: $T=2\pi\sqrt{L/(g-a)}$ • Free fall: $g_{eff}=0$, $T$ infinite (no oscillation)

cards.front: Is the motion of a simple pendulum exactly SHM?
cards.back: No, only approximately for small angles; for large amplitudes the restoring torque is not proportional to $\theta$
cards.hint: Trap: $T=2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ fails for large angles.

cards.front: What does a mechanical wave transport through a medium?
cards.back: Energy (and momentum) and the disturbance, not matter; particles only oscillate about their mean positions
cards.hint: Think of a stadium wave: the wave goes round, people stay in their seats.

cards.front: Mechanical waves vs electromagnetic waves: medium needed?
cards.back: • Mechanical waves need a material medium (sound, waves on string) • EM waves can travel in vacuum (light)

cards.front: What is a transverse wave? Example?
cards.back: Particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation; e.g. wave on a stretched string

cards.front: What is a longitudinal wave? Example?
cards.back: Particles oscillate along the direction of propagation, forming compressions and rarefactions; e.g. sound
cards.hint: Sound in air is always longitudinal.

cards.front: Why can transverse mechanical waves not travel through the bulk of a gas or liquid?
cards.back: They need shear modulus (resistance to shear); fluids have none Longitudinal waves need only bulk modulus, so they travel in solids, liquids and gases

cards.front: Equation of a sinusoidal wave travelling along $+x$?
cards.back: $y(x,t)=a\sin(kx-\omega t+\phi)$ $a$: amplitude, $k$: angular wave number, $\omega$: angular frequency, $\phi$: initial phase
cards.topic: Displacement relation in a progressive wave

cards.front: Direction of the wave $y=a\sin(kx+\omega t)$?
cards.back: Negative $x$ direction
cards.hint: Same signs of $kx$ and $\omega t$ means $-x$; opposite signs means $+x$.
cards.topic: Displacement relation in a progressive wave

cards.front: Define angular wave number. Unit?
cards.back: $k=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$; SI unit $\text{rad m}^{-1}$
cards.topic: Displacement relation in a progressive wave

cards.front: Define wavelength.
cards.back: Minimum distance between two points in the same phase of motion (e.g. crest to adjacent crest)
cards.topic: Displacement relation in a progressive wave

cards.front: Relation between phase difference and path difference?
cards.back: $\Delta\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\,\Delta x$
cards.topic: Displacement relation in a progressive wave

cards.front: Particle velocity vs wave velocity: what is the difference?
cards.back: • Particle velocity $\partial y/\partial t$ varies with time, maximum $a\omega$ • Wave speed $v=\omega/k$ is constant for a medium
cards.hint: Trap: never mix up $a\omega$ (particle) with $\omega/k$ (wave).
cards.topic: Displacement relation in a progressive wave

cards.front: Relation between wave speed, frequency and wavelength?
cards.back: $v=\nu\lambda=\dfrac{\omega}{k}$

cards.front: Speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string?
cards.back: $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$; $T$: tension, $\mu$: mass per unit length
cards.hint: Tension: restoring force; $\mu$: inertia. Same pattern as $\sqrt{\text{elastic}/\text{inertia}}$.

cards.front: Tension in a string is made 4 times. Effect on wave speed?
cards.back: Speed doubles ($v\propto\sqrt{T}$)

cards.front: A wave passes from one medium into another. Which of $\nu$, $\lambda$, $v$ stays the same?
cards.back: Frequency stays the same (set by the source); speed and wavelength change
cards.hint: Wave speed is a property of the medium, not of the source.

cards.front: Speed of longitudinal (sound) wave in a fluid and in a solid rod?
cards.back: • Fluid: $v=\sqrt{B/\rho}$ ($B$: bulk modulus) • Solid rod: $v=\sqrt{Y/\rho}$ ($Y$: Young's modulus)

cards.front: Newton's formula for speed of sound in a gas and its shortcoming?
cards.back: Assumed isothermal process: $v=\sqrt{P/\rho}$ Gives about 280 m/s in air at STP, about 15% less than the measured value

cards.front: Laplace correction for speed of sound in a gas?
cards.back: Process is adiabatic: $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma P}{\rho}}$ With $\gamma=1.4$ for air, $v\approx331$ m/s at STP

cards.front: Speed of sound in an ideal gas in terms of temperature?
cards.back: $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma RT}{M}}$, so $v\propto\sqrt{T}$ ($T$ in kelvin)
cards.hint: Lighter gas (smaller $M$) carries sound faster: faster in $\text{H}_2$ than in $\text{O}_2$.

cards.front: Effect of changing pressure (at constant temperature) on speed of sound in a gas?
cards.back: No effect: $P/\rho$ stays constant at constant temperature
cards.hint: Trap: speed depends on $T$, not on $P$ alone.

cards.front: Absolute temperature of air is made 4 times. Speed of sound?
cards.back: Doubles, since $v\propto\sqrt{T}$

cards.front: Effect of humidity on speed of sound in air?
cards.back: Increases: moist air is less dense than dry air at the same pressure

cards.front: Order of speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases?
cards.back: Solids > liquids > gases
cards.hint: Elastic modulus rises much more than density from gas to solid.

cards.front: State the principle of superposition of waves.
cards.back: When waves overlap, the net displacement is the algebraic sum of the displacements due to each wave: $y=y_1+y_2+\dots$

cards.front: Resultant amplitude of two waves of equal amplitude $a$ with phase difference $\phi$?
cards.back: $A=2a\cos\dfrac{\phi}{2}$
cards.hint: Check: $\phi=2\pi/3$ gives $A=a$.

cards.front: Resultant amplitude for phase difference $0$ and $\pi$ (equal amplitudes $a$)?
cards.back: • $\phi=0$: $2a$ (constructive interference) • $\phi=\pi$: zero (destructive interference)

cards.front: Phase change on reflection at a rigid boundary and at an open boundary?
cards.back: • Rigid (fixed) end: phase change of $\pi$ • Open (free) end: no phase change
cards.hint: A pulse on a string reflected at a fixed end comes back inverted.

cards.front: Incident wave $a\sin(kx-\omega t)$ is reflected at a rigid boundary. Reflected wave?
cards.back: $y_r=a\sin(kx+\omega t+\pi)=-a\sin(kx+\omega t)$

cards.front: Equation of a standing wave formed by two equal waves travelling opposite ways?
cards.back: $y=2a\sin kx\cos\omega t$; amplitude $2a\sin kx$ depends on position
cards.hint: Space part ($\sin kx$) and time part ($\cos\omega t$) are separated: sign of a standing wave.

cards.front: Positions of nodes in the standing wave $y=2a\sin kx\cos\omega t$?
cards.back: $\sin kx=0$: $x=\dfrac{n\lambda}{2}$, $n=0,1,2,\dots$

cards.front: Positions of antinodes in $y=2a\sin kx\cos\omega t$?
cards.back: $|\sin kx|=1$: $x=\left(n+\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\dfrac{\lambda}{2}$

cards.front: Distance between adjacent nodes, and between a node and the next antinode?
cards.back: Node to node: $\lambda/2$; node to antinode: $\lambda/4$
cards.hint: N-A-N-A pattern: each step is $\lambda/4$.

cards.front: How do standing waves differ from travelling waves?
cards.back: • No net transport of energy; waveform does not move • Amplitude varies with position • Particles between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase

cards.front: Allowed frequencies of a string of length $L$ fixed at both ends?
cards.back: $\nu_n=\dfrac{nv}{2L}$, $n=1,2,3,\dots$ (all harmonics); $\lambda_n=2L/n$

cards.front: Fundamental frequency of a stretched string?
cards.back: $\nu_1=\dfrac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$
cards.hint:
Law of length: $
u\propto1/L$; law of tension: $
u\propto\sqrt{T}$; law of mass: $
u\propto1/\sqrt{\mu}$.

cards.front: Number of nodes and antinodes in the $n$th harmonic of a string fixed at both ends?
cards.back: $n+1$ nodes (including both ends) and $n$ antinodes

cards.front: Allowed frequencies of a pipe closed at one end (length $L$)?
cards.back: $ u=\dfrac{(2n-1)v}{4L}$; only odd harmonics: $ u_1, 3 u_1, 5 u_1,\dots$
cards.hint: Closed pipe: only odd. Open pipe and string: all.

cards.front: Allowed frequencies of a pipe open at both ends (length $L$)?
cards.back: $\nu=\dfrac{nv}{2L}$; all harmonics present

cards.front: Ratio of fundamental frequencies of open and closed pipes of the same length?
Second overtone of a closed pipe is which harmonic?
cards.back: Fifth harmonic ($5\nu_1$); in an open pipe the second overtone is the third harmonic
cards.hint: Closed pipe overtones skip even harmonics: 1st, 3rd, 5th...

cards.front: In an air column, what forms at a closed end and at an open end?
cards.back: • Closed end: displacement node (pressure antinode) • Open end: displacement antinode (pressure node)

cards.front: What are beats?
cards.back: Periodic rise and fall (waxing and waning) of loudness when two sounds of slightly different frequencies superpose

cards.front: Beat frequency for two sources of frequencies $\nu_1$ and $\nu_2$?
cards.back: $ u_{beat}=| u_1- u_2|$; time between successive maxima $=1/| u_1- u_2|$
cards.hint: Beats are heard clearly only when the difference is small.

cards.front: Effect of loading a tuning fork with wax, and of filing its prongs?
cards.back: • Loading (wax): frequency decreases • Filing: frequency increases

cards.front: Fork A (256 Hz) gives 4 beats/s with fork B. Loading B raises beats to 6/s. Frequency of B?
cards.back: 252 Hz: loading lowers B; beats rise only if B was already below A
cards.hint: If B were 260 Hz, loading would bring it closer to 256 and reduce beats.

cards.front: Musicians tune an instrument against a standard using beats. How?
cards.back: Adjust tension until the beats disappear (beat frequency zero), so both frequencies are equal

cards.front: Basic nature of electric charge?
cards.back: Scalar; two kinds (positive and negative); like charges repel, unlike attract; SI unit coulomb (C)

cards.front: A glass rod is rubbed with silk. Charges acquired?
cards.back: Glass rod: positive, silk: negative (electrons move from glass to silk)

cards.front: What does a gold-leaf electroscope detect, and how?
cards.back: Detects charge on a body: charge spreads to the leaves, and like charges make the leaves diverge

cards.front: A body becomes positively charged by rubbing. What happened to its mass?
cards.back: It lost electrons, so its mass decreases very slightly
cards.hint: Trap: positive charge comes from losing electrons, not gaining protons.

cards.front: Conductors vs insulators?
cards.back: • Conductors: charges move freely (metals, human body, earth) • Insulators: charges cannot move (glass, plastic, nylon)

cards.front: How is a metal sphere charged by induction using a positive rod?
cards.back: Bring rod near → electrons gather on near side → earth the sphere → remove earthing → remove rod Sphere gets negative charge (opposite to rod)
cards.hint: Remove earth connection before removing the rod.

cards.front: In charging by induction, does the inducing body lose charge?
cards.back: No; there is no contact, so the inducing body keeps its charge

cards.front: What is additivity of charge?
cards.back: Total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of individual charges (signs included)

cards.front: State conservation of charge.
cards.back: Total charge of an isolated system remains constant; charge is only transferred, never created or destroyed

cards.front: What is quantisation of charge?
cards.back: $q=ne$, $n$ an integer, $e=1.602\times10^{-19}$ C (basic unit of charge)
cards.hint: Charge $1.5e$ or $2.5e$ is impossible for a free body.

cards.front: How many electrons make up a charge of $-1$ C?
cards.back: $n=\dfrac{1}{1.6\times10^{-19}}\approx6.25\times10^{18}$ electrons

cards.front: Why can quantisation of charge be ignored at macroscopic level?
cards.back: $e$ is extremely small, so charges of ordinary bodies contain huge $n$ and look continuous

cards.front: State Coulomb's law (formula).
cards.back: $F=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}$, along the line joining the point charges $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}=9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^2\text{C}^{-2}$
cards.hint: Valid for point charges at rest.

cards.front: Value and unit of permittivity of free space $\varepsilon_0$?
cards.back: $\varepsilon_0=8.854\times10^{-12}\ \text{C}^2\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}$

cards.front: Dimensions of $\varepsilon_0$?
cards.hint: $\varepsilon_0=q^2/(Fr^2)$: $A^2T^2$ over $MLT^{-2}\cdot L^2$.

cards.front: Coulomb force between two charges in a medium of dielectric constant $K$?
cards.back: $F=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0K}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2}$, i.e. reduced $K$ times from vacuum
cards.hint: Water has $K\approx80$, so forces drop about 80 times.

cards.front: Distance between two point charges is halved. New force?
cards.back: 4 times ($F\propto1/r^2$)

cards.front: Vector form of Coulomb's law for force on $q_2$ due to $q_1$?
cards.back: $\vec F_{21}=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r_{21}^2}\hat r_{21}$, $\hat r_{21}$ pointing from $q_1$ to $q_2$ $\vec F_{12}=-\vec F_{21}$

cards.front: Ratio of electric to gravitational force between an electron and a proton?
cards.back: About $2.4\times10^{39}$; for two protons about $1.3\times10^{36}$
cards.hint: Independent of distance: both follow inverse square law.

cards.front: Two identical conducting spheres with $q_1$, $q_2$ touch and separate. Charge on each?
cards.back: $\dfrac{q_1+q_2}{2}$ each (signs included)

cards.front: Principle of superposition for electrostatic forces?
cards.back: Net force on a charge is the vector sum of forces due to each other charge, each acting as if the others were absent

cards.front: Charges $q$ and $4q$ are separated by $d$. Where is the net force on a third charge zero?
cards.back: On the line joining them, $d/3$ from $q$ (between them)
cards.hint: Null point for like charges lies between, nearer the smaller charge.

cards.front: Define electric field. SI unit?
cards.back: $\vec E=\vec F/q_0$, force per unit positive test charge ($q_0\to0$) Unit $\text{N C}^{-1}$ (= $\text{V m}^{-1}$)

cards.front: Electric field of a point charge $q$ at distance $r$?
cards.back: $E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2}$, radially outward for $q>0$, inward for $q<0$
cards.hint: Direction: away from +, towards −.

cards.front: Dimensions of electric field?
Why is the test charge taken to be vanishingly small?
cards.back: So it does not disturb the source charges and alter the field being measured

cards.front: An electron and a proton are placed in the same uniform field. Compare force and acceleration.
cards.back: Same magnitude of force, opposite directions Electron's acceleration is about 1836 times larger (smaller mass)

cards.front: Main properties of electrostatic field lines?
cards.back: • Start on + charge, end on − charge (or infinity) • Continuous, never cross • Never form closed loops

cards.front: Why can two electric field lines never cross?
cards.back: At a crossing the field would have two directions at one point, which is impossible

cards.front: What does the density of field lines indicate?
cards.back: Strength of the field: lines crowded where $E$ is strong, far apart where weak

cards.front: Electric flux through a small area $\Delta S$?
cards.back: $\Delta\phi=\vec E\cdot\Delta\vec S=E\,\Delta S\cos\theta$, $\theta$: angle between $\vec E$ and area normal

cards.front: SI unit and dimensions of electric flux?
cards.back: $\text{N m}^2\text{C}^{-1}$ (= V m); dimensions $[ML^3T^{-3}A^{-1}]$

cards.front: Direction of area vector for a closed surface?
cards.back: Along the outward normal; so outgoing field lines give positive flux

cards.front: Define electric dipole moment. Direction and unit?
cards.back: $p=q\cdot2a$, directed from $-q$ to $+q$; SI unit C m
cards.hint: Trap: $\vec p$ points from − to +, opposite to the field lines between the charges.

cards.front: Field of a short dipole on its axial line at distance $r$?
cards.back: $E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2p}{r^3}$, along $\vec p$
cards.hint: Axial gets the 2: $2p$ on axis, $p$ on equator.

cards.front: Field of a short dipole on its equatorial line at distance $r$?
cards.back: $E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^3}$, opposite to $\vec p$

cards.front: Ratio of axial to equatorial field of a short dipole at the same distance?
How does the field of a dipole fall off with distance, compared to a point charge?
cards.back: Dipole: $E\propto1/r^3$ (at large $r$); point charge: $E\propto1/r^2$

cards.front: What is an ideal (point) dipole?
cards.back: Limit $q\to\infty$, $2a\to0$ with $p=q\cdot2a$ finite

cards.front: Torque on a dipole in a uniform electric field?
cards.back: $\vec\tau=\vec p\times\vec E$, magnitude $pE\sin\theta$
cards.hint: Torque tries to align $\vec p$ along $\vec E$.
cards.topic: Dipole in a uniform external field

cards.front: Net force on a dipole in a uniform field, and in a non-uniform field?
cards.back: • Uniform field: net force zero (only torque) • Non-uniform field: net force non-zero
cards.hint: Rubbed comb attracts paper bits: non-uniform field induces and pulls dipoles.
cards.topic: Dipole in a uniform external field

cards.front: At what angle is the torque on a dipole maximum, and when zero?
cards.back: Maximum $pE$ at $\theta=90^\circ$; zero at $\theta=0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$
cards.topic: Dipole in a uniform external field

cards.front: Linear, surface and volume charge densities: symbols and units?
cards.back:
• $\lambda$: $\text{C m}^{-1}$
• $\sigma$: $\text{C m}^{-2}$
• $\rho$: $\text{C m}^{-3}$

cards.front: State Gauss's law.
cards.back: $\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec S=\dfrac{q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$: total flux through a closed surface equals enclosed charge over $\varepsilon_0$

cards.front: Flux through a closed surface when all charges are outside it?
cards.back: Zero
cards.hint: Every line that enters also leaves.

cards.front: A charge $q$ is at the centre of a cube. Flux through one face?
cards.back: $\dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}$ (total $q/\varepsilon_0$ shared by 6 faces by symmetry)
cards.hint: Flux depends only on enclosed charge, not on size or shape of the surface.

cards.front: A charge $q$ is placed at a corner of a cube. Total flux through the cube?
cards.back: $\dfrac{q}{8\varepsilon_0}$: 8 such cubes would enclose the charge completely

cards.front: In Gauss's law, which charges produce the field $\vec E$ in the integral?
cards.back: All charges, inside and outside; but only enclosed charge decides the net flux
cards.hint: Trap: zero flux does not mean zero field on the surface.

cards.front: Can a Gaussian surface pass through a discrete point charge?
cards.back: No; the field is not well defined at the charge's location

cards.front: Field of an infinitely long straight uniformly charged wire?
cards.back: $E=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r}$, radial, $E\propto1/r$
cards.hint: Use a coaxial cylinder as the Gaussian surface.

cards.front: Field of an infinite uniformly charged plane sheet?
cards.back: $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, normal to sheet, independent of distance
cards.hint: Sheet: no $r$ in the answer. Wire: $1/r$. Point: $1/r^2$.

cards.front: Field of a uniformly charged thin spherical shell, outside and inside?
cards.back: • Outside ($r>R$): $E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2}$ (like a point charge at centre) • Inside ($r$E=0$
cards.hint: Hollow shell: field-free inside.

cards.front: Graph of $E$ vs $r$ for a charged thin spherical shell?
cards.back: Zero up to $R$, jumps to $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ at the surface, then falls as $1/r^2$

cards.front: Two parallel infinite sheets carry $+\sigma$ and $-\sigma$. Field between and outside?
cards.back: Between: $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ (from + to −); outside: zero

cards.front: Define electrostatic potential at a point.
cards.back: Work done by an external force per unit positive charge in bringing it slowly from infinity to that point; $V=W/q$

cards.front: SI unit and dimensions of electric potential?
cards.back: Volt, $1\ \text{V}=1\ \text{J C}^{-1}$; dimensions $[ML^2T^{-3}A^{-1}]$

cards.front: Why can potential energy be defined for electrostatic force?
cards.back: Electrostatic force is conservative: work done is path-independent and zero round a closed loop

cards.front: Potential at distance $r$ from a point charge $q$?
cards.back: $V=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r}$ (zero at infinity)
cards.hint: Keep the sign of $q$: negative charge gives negative potential.
cards.topic: Potential due to a point charge

cards.front: If distance from a point charge doubles, what happens to $V$ and $E$?
cards.back: $V$ halves ($\propto1/r$), $E$ becomes one-fourth ($\propto1/r^2$)
cards.topic: Potential due to a point charge

cards.front: Is electric potential a scalar or vector? Net potential of many charges?
cards.back: Scalar; net potential is the algebraic sum $V=\sum\dfrac{q_i}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r_i}$
cards.topic: Potential due to a system of charges

cards.front: Potential of a short dipole at distance $r$, angle $\theta$ from its axis?
cards.back: $V=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p\cos\theta}{r^2}$
cards.hint: $\theta=0$ (axis): maximum; $\theta=90^\circ$ (equator): zero.
cards.topic: Potential due to an electric dipole

cards.front: Potential and field on the equatorial line of a dipole?
cards.back: $V=0$ but $E\neq0$ (field is opposite to $\vec p$)
cards.hint: Trap: zero potential does not mean zero field.
cards.topic: Potential due to an electric dipole

cards.front: How does dipole potential vary with distance, compared to a point charge?
cards.back: Dipole: $V\propto1/r^2$; point charge: $V\propto1/r$
cards.topic: Potential due to an electric dipole

cards.front: Potential of a uniformly charged thin spherical shell, outside and inside?
cards.back: • Outside: $V=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}$ • Inside: constant, $V=\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0R}$ (equal to surface value)
cards.topic: Potential due to a system of charges

cards.front: Inside a charged spherical shell, $E=0$. Is $V$ also zero?
cards.back: No; $V$ is constant and non-zero, equal to its value at the surface
cards.hint: $E=0$ means $V$ does not change, not that $V=0$.
cards.topic: Potential due to a system of charges

cards.front: What is an equipotential surface? Work done moving a charge on it?
cards.back: Surface with the same potential everywhere; work done moving a charge on it is zero

cards.front: Angle between electric field and an equipotential surface?
cards.back: Always $90^\circ$: field is normal to equipotential surfaces
cards.hint: No work along the surface, so no field component along it.

cards.front: Shape of equipotential surfaces for a point charge and for a uniform field?
cards.back: • Point charge: concentric spheres • Uniform field: parallel planes perpendicular to the field

cards.front: Can two equipotential surfaces intersect?
cards.back: No; one point would have two potentials and two field directions

cards.front: Relation between electric field and potential?
cards.back: $E=-\dfrac{dV}{dr}$; $\vec E$ points along the steepest decrease of potential
cards.hint: Field points 'downhill' in potential.

cards.front: Where equipotential surfaces are closer together, what is the field like?
cards.back: Stronger, since $|E|=|\Delta V|/\Delta r$

cards.front: Potential energy of two point charges $q_1$, $q_2$ separated by $r$?
cards.back: $U=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r}$; positive for like charges, negative for unlike
cards.hint: Trap: $U\propto1/r$, not $1/r^2$.
cards.topic: Potential energy of a system of charges

cards.front: Potential energy of a system of three point charges?
cards.back: Sum over all pairs: $U=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r_{12}}+\dfrac{q_1q_3}{r_{13}}+\dfrac{q_2q_3}{r_{23}}\right)$
cards.hint: $n$ charges give $n(n-1)/2$ pairs.
cards.topic: Potential energy of a system of charges

cards.front: Potential energy of a charge $q$ placed in an external potential $V(\vec r)$?
cards.back: $U=qV(\vec r)$
cards.topic: Potential energy in an external field

cards.front: Define electron volt. Value in joules?
cards.back: Energy gained by an electron accelerated through 1 V: $1\ \text{eV}=1.6\times10^{-19}$ J
cards.topic: Potential energy in an external field

cards.front: Potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field at angle $\theta$?
cards.back: $U=-pE\cos\theta=-\vec p\cdot\vec E$ (zero taken at $\theta=90^\circ$)
cards.topic: Potential energy of a dipole in an external field

cards.front: Stable and unstable equilibrium positions of a dipole in a uniform field?
cards.back: • Stable: $\theta=0$, $U=-pE$ (minimum) • Unstable: $\theta=180^\circ$, $U=+pE$ (maximum)
cards.topic: Potential energy of a dipole in an external field

cards.front: Work done to rotate a dipole from $\theta=0$ to $\theta=180^\circ$ in a uniform field?
cards.back: $W=2pE$ ($U$ changes from $-pE$ to $+pE$)
cards.topic: Potential energy of a dipole in an external field

cards.front: Electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium?
cards.back: Zero everywhere inside the conductor
cards.hint: Free electrons would move if any field existed inside.

cards.front: Where does excess charge on a conductor reside?
cards.back: Only on its surface (the outer surface when no charge sits in a cavity); net charge inside the volume is zero
cards.hint: Gauss's law with $E=0$ inside gives zero enclosed charge.

cards.front: Direction of electrostatic field just outside a charged conductor's surface?
cards.back: Normal to the surface; otherwise surface charges would move

cards.front: Potential within the volume of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium?
cards.back: Constant throughout and equal to its surface value

cards.front: Field just outside a charged conductor with surface charge density $\sigma$?
cards.back: $E=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$, along the outward normal
cards.hint: Trap: not $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$ (that is for an isolated thin sheet).

cards.front: What is electrostatic shielding?
cards.back: Field inside a charge-free cavity of a conductor is zero whatever the outside charges and fields E.g. safer to sit inside a car during a thunderstorm

cards.front: Free charges vs bound charges?
cards.back: • Conductors: free electrons move through the material • Dielectrics: bound charges can only shift slightly within atoms/molecules

cards.front: Polar vs non-polar molecules, with examples?
cards.back: • Polar: permanent dipole moment (e.g. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, HCl) • Non-polar: zero dipole moment without field (e.g. $\text{O}_2$, $\text{H}_2$)

cards.front: Define polarisation $\vec P$ of a dielectric.
cards.back: Dipole moment per unit volume; for linear isotropic dielectrics $\vec P=\chi_e\vec E$ ($\chi_e$: electric susceptibility)

cards.front: Why is the field inside a dielectric less than the applied field?
cards.back: Polarisation creates surface bound charges whose field opposes the applied field: $E=E_0/K$

cards.front: Define dielectric constant $K$. Its value for vacuum and for a metal?
cards.back: $K=\varepsilon/\varepsilon_0$ (also $C/C_0$); $K=1$ for vacuum, $K=\infty$ for a metal

cards.front: Define capacitance. SI unit?
cards.back: $C=\dfrac{Q}{V}$; unit farad ($1\ \text{F}=1\ \text{C V}^{-1}$), a very large unit
cards.hint: Practical units: $\mu\text{F}$, nF, pF.

cards.front: Dimensions of capacitance?
On what does capacitance depend?
cards.back: Geometry (size, shape, separation) and the medium between plates; not on $Q$ or $V$

cards.front: Capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor (vacuum)?
cards.back: $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$; $A$: plate area, $d$: separation
cards.hint: $C\propto A$ and $C\propto1/d$: halve $d$, double $C$.

cards.front: Field between and outside the plates of a parallel plate capacitor?
cards.back: Between: uniform, $E=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$; outside: zero (ignoring fringing)

cards.front: Capacitance when the space is completely filled by a dielectric $K$?
cards.back: $C=\dfrac{K\varepsilon_0A}{d}$, i.e. $K$ times larger

cards.front: Capacitance with a dielectric slab of thickness $t<d$ between the plates?
cards.back: $C=\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d-t+\dfrac{t}{K}}$
cards.hint: Metal slab: put $K=\infty$, giving $\varepsilon_0A/(d-t)$.

cards.front: Dielectric inserted with battery still connected. Effect on $V$, $Q$, $C$, $U$?
cards.back: $V$ same; $C\to KC$, $Q\to KQ$, $U\to KU$

cards.front: Dielectric inserted after disconnecting the battery. Effect on $Q$, $V$, $E$, $U$?
cards.back: $Q$ same; $V\to V/K$, $E\to E/K$, $U\to U/K$
cards.hint: Battery off: $Q$ fixed. Battery on: $V$ fixed.

cards.front: Equivalent capacitance of capacitors in series? What is common?
cards.back: $\dfrac{1}{C}=\dfrac{1}{C_1}+\dfrac{1}{C_2}+\dots$; same charge on each
cards.hint: Series $C$ is smaller than the smallest one.

cards.front: Equivalent capacitance of capacitors in parallel? What is common?
cards.back: $C=C_1+C_2+\dots$; same potential difference across each

cards.front: $n$ identical capacitors $C$: ratio of parallel to series equivalent capacitance?
cards.back: Parallel $nC$, series $C/n$: ratio $n^2$
cards.hint: Capacitors combine opposite to resistors.

cards.front: Energy stored in a charged capacitor?
cards.back: $U=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}=\tfrac{1}{2}CV^2=\tfrac{1}{2}QV$
cards.hint: Use $Q^2/2C$ when $Q$ is fixed and $\tfrac12CV^2$ when $V$ is fixed.

cards.front: Energy density of an electric field in vacuum?
cards.back: $u=\tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0E^2$ (energy per unit volume)

cards.front: Two capacitors charged to $V_1$, $V_2$ are joined (like plates together). Common potential?
cards.back: $V=\dfrac{C_1V_1+C_2V_2}{C_1+C_2}$; charge is conserved but energy is lost
cards.hint: Loss $=\dfrac{C_1C_2(V_1-V_2)^2}{2(C_1+C_2)}$, as heat and radiation.

cards.front: Define electric current. What is its SI unit?
cards.back: Rate of flow of charge through a cross-section: $I = \dfrac{dq}{dt}$. SI unit: ampere (A) = $\text{C s}^{-1}$.

cards.front: Current has a direction. Is it a vector or a scalar?
cards.back: Scalar. Currents meeting at a junction add algebraically, not by the vector law of addition.
cards.hint: Trap: having a direction does not make a quantity a vector.

cards.front: What is current density? Give its SI unit and nature.
cards.back: Current per unit area normal to the flow: $j = \dfrac{I}{A}$. A vector, SI unit $\text{A m}^{-2}$.
cards.hint: General form: $I = \vec{j}\cdot\vec{A}$.

cards.front: How is the conventional current direction related to electron flow?
cards.back: Conventional current is along the flow of positive charge, i.e. opposite to the direction of electron drift.

cards.front: State Ohm's law.
cards.back: At constant temperature (physical conditions), current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference: $V = IR$.

cards.front: How does resistance of a uniform wire depend on its dimensions?
cards.back: $R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A}$: $R \propto$ length $l$, $R \propto \dfrac{1}{A}$; $\rho$ = resistivity of the material.

cards.front: A wire is stretched to n times its length (volume constant). What is its new resistance?
cards.back: $n^2 R$. Length becomes $nl$ and area $A/n$, so $R \propto \dfrac{l}{A} \propto l^2$.
cards.hint: At constant volume: $R \propto l^2$ and $R \propto \dfrac{1}{r^4}$.

cards.front: A wire is drawn so its radius halves (volume constant). New resistance?
cards.back: 16 R, since at constant volume $R \propto \dfrac{1}{r^4}$ (area becomes 1/4, length 4 times).

cards.front: Dimensions of electrical resistance?
cards.back: $[ML^2T^{-3}A^{-2}]$, from $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$ with $V = \dfrac{W}{q}$.

cards.front: SI unit and dimensions of resistivity? On what does it depend?
cards.back: $\Omega\,\text{m}$, $[ML^3T^{-3}A^{-2}]$. Depends only on the material and temperature, not on length or area.
cards.hint: Trap: cutting a wire in half halves R but leaves ρ unchanged.

cards.front: What is conductivity? Write Ohm's law in vector form.
cards.back: $\sigma = \dfrac{1}{\rho}$, SI unit $\text{S m}^{-1}$ ($\Omega^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}$). Vector form: $\vec{j} = \sigma\vec{E}$.

cards.front: Order of resistivity of metals vs insulators?
cards.back: • Metals: $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-6}\ \Omega\,\text{m}$ • Insulators: about $10^{22}$ times (or more) larger • Semiconductors: in between

cards.front: Formula for drift velocity of electrons in a field E?
cards.back: $v_d = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m}$ (magnitude), opposite to $\vec{E}$; $\tau$ = average relaxation time between collisions, $m$ = electron mass.

cards.front: Relation between current and drift velocity?
cards.back: $I = neAv_d$; $n$ = free electron number density, $A$ = cross-section area.

cards.front: What is the average velocity of free electrons in a conductor with no applied field?
cards.back: Zero. Thermal velocities are random in direction, so no net flow of charge.

cards.front: Drift speed is only about mm/s. Why does a bulb glow almost instantly when switched on?
cards.back: The electric field is set up along the whole wire at nearly the speed of light, so free electrons everywhere start drifting at once.
cards.hint: Typical $v_d \sim 10^{-4}$ to $10^{-3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

cards.front: Define mobility. Give its formula and SI unit.
cards.back: Drift speed per unit field: $\mu = \dfrac{v_d}{E} = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}$. SI unit: $\text{m}^2\text{V}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$.

cards.front: Resistivity in terms of microscopic quantities?
cards.back: $\rho = \dfrac{m}{ne^2\tau}$, so $\sigma = \dfrac{ne^2\tau}{m}$.
cards.hint: Larger n or longer τ means lower resistivity.

cards.front: Steady current flows through a wire of non-uniform cross-section. Which quantities are the same everywhere?
cards.back: Only current I is the same. Current density $j$, field $E$ and drift speed $v_d$ all vary as $\dfrac{1}{A}$.
cards.hint: Narrower part: higher drift speed.

cards.front: At fixed applied V, how does drift speed depend on wire length and area?
cards.back: $v_d = \dfrac{eV\tau}{ml}$: $v_d \propto \dfrac{1}{l}$ and independent of area. Doubling $l$ halves $v_d$.
cards.hint: Trap: at fixed V, a thicker wire carries more current but the drift speed is unchanged.

cards.front: Name the three kinds of deviation from Ohm's law listed in NCERT.
cards.back: • V stops being proportional to I (non-linear) • Relation depends on the sign of V (e.g. diode) • Relation is not unique: same I for more than one V (e.g. GaAs)

cards.front: Describe the V–I graph of an ohmic conductor. What does its slope give?
cards.back: A straight line through the origin. Slope of V vs I = R; slope of I vs V = $\dfrac{1}{R}$.

cards.front: Graphs of I (y-axis) vs V (x-axis) for a metal wire at T₁ and T₂: the T₁ line is steeper. Which temperature is higher?
cards.back: $T_2$. Smaller slope of I vs V means larger R, and a metal's R rises with temperature.
cards.hint: Trap: check which axis is which. On a V vs I graph the steeper line has the larger R.

cards.front: How does resistivity of a metal vary with temperature (limited range)?
cards.back: $\rho_T = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$; $\alpha$ = temperature coefficient of resistivity, unit $\text{K}^{-1}$ (or $^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$).

cards.front: Sign of the temperature coefficient α for metals vs semiconductors?
cards.back: • Metals: positive (ρ increases with T) • Semiconductors and insulators: negative (ρ decreases with T)

cards.front: Why does the resistivity of a metal increase with temperature?
cards.back: Electrons collide more often, so relaxation time τ decreases; n stays nearly constant. Hence $\rho = \dfrac{m}{ne^2\tau}$ rises.

cards.front: Why does resistivity of a semiconductor decrease with temperature?
cards.back: Number density n increases with temperature, and this outweighs the decrease in τ.

cards.front: Why are nichrome, manganin and constantan used for standard resistors?
cards.back: High resistivity and very weak dependence of resistivity on temperature. Nichrome is also used in heating elements.

cards.front: Shape of the ρ vs T graph for copper?
cards.back: Nearly linear over a wide range around room temperature; at low temperatures it curves and tends to a finite value as T → 0 K.
cards.hint: Trap: ρ of a normal metal does not drop to zero at 0 K.

cards.front: Three formulas for power dissipated in a resistor?
cards.back: $P = VI = I^2R = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$. SI unit: watt.
cards.hint: Series (same I): use $I^2R$. Parallel (same V): use $\dfrac{V^2}{R}$.

cards.front: A 100 W and a 60 W bulb (same rated V) are in series. Which glows brighter?
cards.back: The 60 W bulb. $R = \dfrac{V^2}{P}$ is larger for it, and with the same current $P = I^2R$ is larger.
cards.hint: In parallel the 100 W bulb glows brighter.

cards.front: Power P is sent through cables of resistance R_c at voltage V. What is the power wasted?
cards.back: $P_c = \dfrac{P^2R_c}{V^2}$. So power is transmitted at very high voltage to cut losses.

cards.front: How many joules make 1 kWh?
cards.back: $1\ \text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6\ \text{J}$. kWh is a unit of energy, not power.

cards.front: Define the emf of a cell.
cards.back: Potential difference between the terminals when no current is drawn (open circuit); work done per unit charge by the cell. Unit: volt.
cards.hint: Despite its name, emf is not a force.

cards.front: Terminal voltage and current when a cell (ε, r) drives an external resistor R?
cards.back: $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R + r}$ and $V = \varepsilon - Ir$.

cards.front: Maximum current that a cell of emf ε and internal resistance r can give?
cards.back: On short circuit ($R = 0$): $I_{max} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{r}$.

cards.front: When is the terminal voltage of a cell greater than its emf?
cards.back: While it is being charged: current enters the + terminal and $V = \varepsilon + Ir$.
cards.hint: Discharging: V < ε. Open circuit: V = ε.

cards.front: Graph of terminal voltage V vs current I drawn from a cell?
cards.back: Straight line with slope $-r$. V-intercept = ε; I-intercept = $\dfrac{\varepsilon}{r}$ (short-circuit current).

cards.front: For what load R is the power delivered by a cell (ε, r) maximum?
cards.back: When $R = r$. Then $P_{max} = \dfrac{\varepsilon^2}{4r}$.

cards.front: Equivalent emf and internal resistance of two cells in series?
cards.back: $\varepsilon_{eq} = \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2$, $r_{eq} = r_1 + r_2$. If one cell is reversed: $\varepsilon_{eq} = \varepsilon_1 - \varepsilon_2$, $r_{eq}$ unchanged.

cards.front: Equivalent emf and internal resistance of two cells in parallel?
cards.back: $\varepsilon_{eq} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_1 r_2 + \varepsilon_2 r_1}{r_1 + r_2}$, $r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1 r_2}{r_1 + r_2}$.
cards.hint: If a cell is reversed, replace its ε by −ε.

cards.front: n identical cells (ε, r) are joined in parallel. Equivalent emf and internal resistance?
cards.back: $\varepsilon_{eq} = \varepsilon$ and $r_{eq} = \dfrac{r}{n}$.

cards.front: n identical cells are in series but one is connected in reverse. Net emf and internal resistance?
cards.back: Emf = $(n - 2)\varepsilon$ (the reversed cell cancels one other); internal resistance stays $nr$.
cards.hint: Trap: reversing a cell changes the emf, not the internal resistance.

cards.front: Equivalent resistance of resistors in series and in parallel?
cards.back:
• Series: $R = R_1 + R_2 + \dots$ (same current)
• Parallel: $\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \dots$ (same voltage)
cards.hint: Parallel combination is smaller than the smallest resistor.

cards.front: State Kirchhoff's junction rule. Which law is it based on?
cards.back: Sum of currents entering a junction = sum leaving. Based on conservation of charge.

cards.front: State Kirchhoff's loop rule. Which law is it based on?
cards.back: Algebraic sum of changes in potential around any closed loop is zero. Based on conservation of energy.

cards.front: Sign convention for the loop rule when going round a loop?
cards.back: • Across R along the current: $-IR$ (against: $+IR$) • Through a cell from − to + terminal: $+\varepsilon$ (from + to −: $-\varepsilon$)

cards.front: Wheatstone bridge: R₁, R₂ in one branch, R₃, R₄ in the other; R₁ and R₃ meet at one battery terminal. Balance condition?
cards.back: $\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = \dfrac{R_3}{R_4}$, with no current through the galvanometer.
cards.hint: Ratio of resistances in one branch equals ratio in the other.

cards.front: Does the galvanometer's resistance affect the balance of a Wheatstone bridge?
cards.back: No. At balance no current flows in that arm, so it can be removed. Interchanging cell and galvanometer also keeps the bridge balanced.

cards.front: Working principle and formula of a metre bridge?
cards.back: Works on the Wheatstone bridge principle. With null point at $l_1$ cm from the end next to R: $R = S\,\dfrac{l_1}{100 - l_1}$.

cards.front: Why should the null point of a metre bridge be near the middle of the wire?
cards.back: It minimises the percentage error in R and reduces the effect of end resistances.

cards.front: What did Oersted observe in 1820?
cards.back: A current-carrying wire deflects a nearby compass needle: moving charges (currents) produce a magnetic field.

cards.front: Shape and direction of field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire?
cards.back: Concentric circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it. Direction by the right-hand thumb rule (thumb along current, fingers curl along B).
cards.hint: Reversing the current reverses the compass deflection.

cards.front: Write the Lorentz force on a charge q moving with velocity v in fields E and B.
cards.back: $\vec{F} = q[\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B}]$

cards.front: Magnitude of magnetic force on a moving charge? When is it zero?
cards.back: $F = qvB\sin\theta$. Zero when the charge is at rest or moves parallel/antiparallel to B.
cards.hint: Force is perpendicular to both v and B.

cards.front: How much work does a magnetic field do on a moving charge?
cards.back: Zero. The force is always perpendicular to velocity, so speed and kinetic energy stay constant; only direction changes.
cards.hint: Trap: a magnetic field cannot speed up or slow down a charge.

cards.front: SI unit of magnetic field B and its relation to gauss?
cards.hint: Earth's field at the surface is about $10^{-5}\ \text{T}$.

cards.front: Dimensions of magnetic field B?
Force on a straight conductor of length l carrying current I in a uniform field B?
cards.back: $\vec{F} = I\vec{l} \times \vec{B}$, magnitude $BIl\sin\theta$; $\vec{l}$ points along the current.

cards.front: Net magnetic force on a closed current loop of any shape in a uniform field?
cards.back: Zero. (A torque may still act on it.)

cards.front: A bent wire carries current I from point P to Q in a uniform B. What is the force on it?
cards.back: Same as on a straight wire from P to Q: $\vec{F} = I\,\vec{PQ} \times \vec{B}$. Shape does not matter in a uniform field.
cards.hint: A semicircular wire feels the same force as its diameter.

cards.front: Radius of the circular path of a charge moving perpendicular to a uniform B?
cards.back: $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$, from $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. Radius $\propto$ momentum.

cards.front: Angular frequency and period of a charge circling in a uniform B?
cards.back: $\omega = \dfrac{qB}{m}$, $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$. Both are independent of speed and radius.
cards.hint: Faster particles move in bigger circles but take the same time per revolution.

cards.front: Radius of circular path in terms of kinetic energy K?
cards.back: $r = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}$. For equal K, $r \propto \dfrac{\sqrt{m}}{q}$.

cards.front: A proton and an α-particle enter the same B at right angles with equal kinetic energy. Ratio of radii?
cards.back: 1 : 1. $r \propto \dfrac{\sqrt{m}}{q}$: α has $\sqrt{4m}/2e = \sqrt{m}/e$, same as the proton.
cards.hint: Same momentum instead? r ∝ 1/q, so r_p : r_α = 2 : 1.

cards.front: Path of a charged particle entering a uniform B at angle θ (0 < θ < 90°)?
cards.back: A helix. $v\sin\theta$ gives circular motion; $v\cos\theta$ (along B) is unchanged.
cards.hint: θ = 0°: straight line. θ = 90°: circle.

cards.front: Pitch of the helical path of a charge in a uniform B?
cards.back: $p = v_\parallel T = \dfrac{2\pi m v\cos\theta}{qB}$; radius $r = \dfrac{mv\sin\theta}{qB}$.

cards.front: An electron and a proton enter a uniform B perpendicularly with the same speed. How do their paths differ?
cards.back: Radius ratio $r_e : r_p = m_e : m_p$, so the electron's circle is much smaller; they circle in opposite senses.

cards.front: Condition for a charge to pass undeflected through crossed E and B fields?
cards.back: $v = \dfrac{E}{B}$ (electric and magnetic forces cancel: $qE = qvB$). Works as a velocity selector.
cards.hint: Independent of the charge and mass of the particle.

cards.front: State the Biot–Savart law.
cards.back: $dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2}$; in vector form $d\vec{B} \propto I\,d\vec{l} \times \vec{r}/r^3$. $\theta$ is between $d\vec{l}$ and $\vec{r}$.

cards.front: Value and unit of μ₀ (permeability of free space)?
Magnetic field due to a current element at a point on its own axis (along dl)?
